15   Configuring MPLS
Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) is a label switching technology that provides the ability to set up 
connection-oriented paths over a connectionless IP network. MPLS sets up a specific path for a sequence 
of packets. The packets are identified by a label inserted into each packet.
This implementation of MPLS provides the network architecture that is needed to set up Layer 2 Virtual 
Private Network (VPN) that uses MPLS labels to transport data. L2 VPNs provide multiple types of 
Layer2 services to the user like Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) that allows E-LAN connectivity 
services over the MPLS network, and VPWS (Virtual Private Wire Service) that provides E-LINE (point 
to point) connectivity.
The MPLS architecture provided is based on the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). The LDP consists of a 
set of procedures used by participating Label Switching Routers (LSRs) to define Label Switched Paths 
(LSPs), also referred to as MPLS tunnels. These tunnels provide the foundation necessary to provision 
VPLS.
This chapter documents the OmniSwitch implementation of an LDP-based MPLS network architecture.
For information about how to configure VPLS and VPWS, see Chapter 16, “Configuring Layer 2 VPN 
Services (VPLS, VPWS).”.
In This Chapter
This chapter describes the basic components of MPLS and how to configure them through the Command 
Line Interface (CLI). CLI commands are used in the configuration examples; for more details about the 
syntax of commands, see the OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 CLI Reference Guide.
The following information and procedures are included in this chapter:
• “MPLS Defaults” on page 15-2
• “Quick Steps for Configuring MPLS” on page 15-3
• “MPLS Overview” on page 15-6
• “Configuring MPLS” on page 15-12
• “MPLS Ping and Traceroute” on page 15-15
• “Verifying the MPLS and LDP Configuration” on page 15-18
• “MPLS Configuration Example” on page 15-19

Quick Steps for Configuring MPLS
The following prerequisites for configuring the MPLS network are required on each router that will 
participate as a Label Edge Router (LER) or Label Switch Router (LSR) in the network:
• AOS supports installation or removal of AOS MPLS package. MPLS is packaged into a Debian 
package that can be installed on the switch. To configure MPLS in AOS, it is required to install the 
MPLS package using Package Manager commands. For more information on the package installation 
commands, see “Chassis Management and Monitoring Commands” chapter in the OmniSwitch AOS 
Release 8 CLI Reference Guide.
• To enable MPLS interface, either a Site or Node license is required to be installed on the switch. For 
more information on the Site and Node Based Licensing for MPLS configuration commands and 
detailed steps, see “Chassis Management and Monitoring Commands” chapter in the OmniSwitch AOS 
Release 8 CLI Reference Guide, and “Managing System Files” chapter in OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 
Switch Management Guide.
• The IP configuration required to provide a stable IP network topology on which MPLS tunnels will 
traverse. This includes the VLAN-port associations and IP interface configuration required to provide 
the necessary connections between participating LSRs.
• A Loopback0 interface that will serve as the system IP address to identify the router as an MPLS 
router.
• At least one IP interface that will serve as an MPLS interface running the Label Distribution Protocol 
(LDP) protocol.
1 Use the ip interface command to configure the Loopback0 interface. A Loopback0 IP interface must 
be explicitly configured on the router for MPLS functionality to become operational. For example:
-> ip interface Loopback0 address 1.1.1.1
2 Setup routing for the interfaces. For example:
-> ip interface vlan10 address 10.0.0.1/24 vlan 10
-> ip load ospf 
-> ip ospf interface vlan10
-> ip ospf area 0.0.0.0
-> ip ospf admin-state enable
-> ip ospf interface vlan10 area 0.0.0.0 
-> ip ospf interface vlan10 admin-state enable
3 Enable MPLS instance on the switch using the mpls interface command. For example:
-> mpls interface vlan10 admin-state enable

OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide

MPLS Overview
MPLS (Multi-Protocol Label Switching) is a form of network transport using hop by hop label switching 
to build point to point connections. An MPLS header is a 32-bit field where 20 bits are the Label ID itself.   
Routers, or in this case Label Switch Routers (LSR), identify the forwarding path by analyzing the Label 
to find the next-hop information. The path formed by a multitude of LSRs to transport frames to a specific 
destination is called an LSP. LSP can be configured in multiple ways, the most popular of them being 
signaling protocols that partially automate the process. 
MPLS directs a flow of IP packets along a Label Switched Path (LSP). LSPs are simplex, meaning that the 
traffic flows in one direction (unidirectional) from an ingress router to an egress router. Two LSPs are 
required for duplex traffic. Each LSP carries traffic in a specific direction, forwarding packets from one 
router to the next across the MPLS domain.
When an ingress router receives a packet, it adds an MPLS header to the packet and forwards it to the next 
hop in the LSP. The labeled packet is forwarded along the LSP path until it reaches the egress router 
(destination point). The MPLS header is removed and the packet is forwarded based on Layer 3 informa-
tion such as the IP destination address. The physical path of the LSP is not constrained to the shortest path 
that the IGP would choose to reach the destination IP address.
MPLS Label Stack
MPLS requires a set of procedures to enhance network layer packets with label stacks which thereby turns 
them into labeled packets. Routers that support MPLS are known as Label Switching Routers (LSRs). In 
order to transmit a labeled packet on a particular data link, an LSR must support the encoding technique 
which, when given a label stack and a network layer packet, produces a labeled packet.
In MPLS, packets can carry not just one label, but a set of labels in a stack. An LSR can swap the label at 
the top of the stack, pop the stack, or swap the label and push one or more labels into the stack. Labeled 
packet processing is independent of the level of hierarchy. Processing is always based on the top label in 
the stack which includes information about the operations to perform on the packet's label stack.
The processing of a labeled packet is completely independent of the level of hierarchy. The processing is 
always based on the top label, without regard for the possibility that some number of other labels may 
have been above it in the past, or that some number of other labels may be below it at present.
The label value at the top of the stack is looked up when a labeled packet is received. A successful lookup 
reveals:
• The next hop where the packet is to be forwarded.
• The operation to be performed on the label stack before forwarding.
In addition, the lookup may reveal outgoing data link encapsulation and other information needed to prop-
erly forward the packet.
Label Switching Router
When MPLS is implemented, this feature will function as an LSR (Label Switching Router) or LER 
(Label Edge Router). An LSR uses labels to forward user traffic through the core network. Labels can be 
set up automatically or statically. Automatic set up is possible using signaling protocols like LDP and 
RSVP. MPLS core network consists of multiple such Interconnected LSRs and traffic is forwarded 
through the network using Label switched paths (LSPs). These LSPs originate and terminate on LERs. 
LSPs can be thought of as unidirectional tunnels from one LER to another LER.

<<<PAGE 458>>>
Configuring MPLS
MPLS Overview
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 15-7
Label Edge Router
LERs (Label Edge Router) provide Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) service and forward VPN traffic 
through LSPs. L2 VPNs such as VPWS (Virtual Private Wire Service) and VPLS (Virtual Private LAN 
Service) will be supported along with L3 VPN and EVPN on the edge of the MPLS network. VPLS and 
VPWS will use LDP as the signaling protocol to create service instances on the LER. In addition, VPLS 
can use BGP for discovering VPLS instances.
Signaled LSP
LSPs are set up using a signaling protocol, such as the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). The signaling 
protocol allows labels to be assigned from an ingress router to the egress router. Signaling is triggered by 
the ingress routers. Configuration is required only on the ingress router and is not required on intermedi-
ate routers. Signaling also facilitates path selection.
A signaled LSP is confined to one IGP area for LSPs using constrained-path. They cannot cross an auton-
omous system (AS) boundary.
Label Distribution Protocol
The LDP protocol (Label Distribution Protocol) is used in MPLS network which generates and exchanges 
labels between neighboring routers. It is the set of messages exchanged by LSRs (Label Switched Rout-
ers) to establish LSPs (Label Switched Paths). A LSP is a path taken by all packets that belong to the 
Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) corresponding to that LSP.
Whenever a new router comes up, it sends out a hello packet to all routers multicast group addresses. 
Every router directly connected to the network receives the packet. Receipt of a hello packet from another 
LSR creates a Hello Adjacency with that LSR. These hello packets are sent using UDP protocol. LDP 
hello packets carries an identifier (LSR ID), the LSR intends to use. An Extended Discovery mechanism is 
also used to locate LSRs that are not directly connected which is referred as Targeted peer. 
In this way, adjacencies are formed between two neighboring routers, which opens a way for the session 
to be established between them. This session establishment is carried out using TCP handshake. Upon 
successful session establishment, two LSRs become LDP peers and exchanges advertisement messages.
Two kinds of notification messages are used in LDP to provide advisory information and to inform error 
information. An LSR maintains a hold timer with each Hello adjacency and if the timer expires without 
receiving a matching hello packet from the peer, LSR concludes that the peer is no longer alive and then 
deletes the Hello adjacency with that peer by sending a Notification message and closing the transport 
connection. Similarly, a keepalive timer is used to monitor the integrity of the established session. If this 
timer expires, the LSR concludes that the transport connection is bad or that the peer has failed, and it 
terminates the LDP session by closing the transport connection.
Label Mapping message is used by an LSR to distribute a label mapping for a FEC to an LDP peer. An 
LSR is responsible for the consistency of the label mappings it has distributed and that its peers have these 
mappings.

label encapsulation.

MPLS Based VPN
An MPLS based network is used as a backbone to provide VPN service. VPLS, VPWS, L3VPN, EVPN 
are the possible services that can be configured on top of an MPLS based network to setup virtual private 
networks. This will allow multiple customer sites (CE) to be connected in a single domain over an IP/
MPLS network. 
LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) and RSVP based MPLS will be used to set up label switched paths 
(LSPs) to interconnect customer sites. These LSPs are also referred to as MPLS tunnels. These tunnels 
form the basis of any multipoint service (L3 VPN or VPLS). 
MPLS Edge refers to an LER or PE (Provider Edge) device, which is connected on one side to the 
customer equipment (CE) device and on the other side the MPLS core network. They originate and termi-
nate LSPs and transport user traffic through them. Since LSPs are essentially tunnels between one PE to 
another PE, these devices allow the creation of Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) for the users. 
Figure 15-2 : MPLS Based VPN

MPLS Overview
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide

L2 VPN
L2 VPNs provide multiple types of Layer 2 services to the user. VPWS provides E-LINE (point to point) 
connectivity whereas VPLS allows E-LAN connectivity services over the MPLS network.
Virtual Private LAN Service
A VPLS service provides connectivity between two or more Service Access Points (SAPs) on one router 
(a local service) or on multiple routers (a distributed service). The connection appears to be a bridged 
domain to the customer sites, so protocols, including routing protocols, can traverse the VPLS service.
VPLS is provided over an IP/MPLS network architecture, which is based on the Label Distribution Proto-
col (LDP). This protocol consists of a set of procedures used by participating Label Switching Routers 
(LSRs) to define Label Switched Paths (LSPs), also referred to as MPLS tunnels. These tunnels provide 
the foundation necessary to provision VPLS.
Virtual Private Wire Service
VPWS is a class of VPN service that provides point-to-point (P2P) VPN connectivity service for custom-
ers connected to an MPLS network. Based on the MPLS technology, VPWS allows multiple customers to 
share one transport leased line (LSP) and creates an exclusive virtual channel for each customer on the 
shared LSP. On an Ethernet network, sites in different cities can communicate over a P2P VPWS connec-
tion on an MPLS network, just like communicating within a Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN).

<<<PAGE 462>>>
Configuring MPLS
MPLS Overview
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 15-11
Graceful Restart on Switches with Redundant CMMs
OmniSwitch supports redundancy if the MASTER goes off-line for any reason. When a takeover occurs, 
an MPLS router re-establishes full adjacencies with all its previously fully adjacent neighbors. This time 
period between the restart and the re-establishment of adjacencies is termed graceful restart.
MPLS provides a graceful restart mechanism for the LDP component of MPLS. This mechanism is 
supported only for planned takeovers (for example, the users performs the takeover), not unplanned take-
overs (for example, the primary CMM unexpectedly fails) or when a link goes down between the two 
routers.
In the network illustration below, a helper router, Router Y monitors the network for topology changes. As 
long as there are none, it continues to advertise its LDP adjacencies as if the restarting router, Router X, 
had remained in continuous LDP operation (that is, Router Y continues to list an adjacency to Router X 
over network segment S, regardless of the adjacency’s current synchronization state.
Figure 15-3 : LDP Graceful Restart Helping and Restarting Router Example
If the restarting router, Router X, was the Designated Router (DR) on network segment S when the help-
ing relationship began, the helper neighbor, Router Y, maintains Router X as the DR until the helping 
relationship is terminated. If there are multiple adjacencies with the restarting Router X, Router Y will act 
as a helper on all other adjacencies.

Configuring MPLS
Enabling or Disabling MPLS
To configure MPLS functionality on a specified IPv4 interface, use mpls interface command. This 
command can be used to enable or disable the administrative status of the MPLS interface. By default, the 
MPLS interface is administratively disabled when the interface is created.
On enabling the MPLS interface, label switching capability is enabled on that specified interface. 
-> mpls interface vlan10 admin-state enable
On disabling MPLS interface, corresponding LDP interface, if any, will be operationally down.
-> mpls interface vlan10 admin-state disable
Use the no form of this command to remove the MPLS interface. On deleting the MPLS interface, it 
deletes the corresponding LDP interface, if any, as well.
-> no mpls interface vlan10
Loading LDP Software 
To load LDP protocol software on the switch, use the mpls load ldp command. MPLS package has to be 
installed before executing this command.
-> mpls load ldp
Enabling or Disabling LDP
To enable or disable the administration status of LDP on the router, use mpls ldp admin-state command. 
LDP must be loaded on the switch to enable LDP on the switch.
-> mpls ldp admin-state enable
-> mpls ldp admin-state disable
Note.  MPLS package has to be installed before executing this command. For package installation 
commands, see the “Chassis Management and Monitoring Commands” chapter in the OmniSwitch AOS 
Release 8 Switch Management Guide.

<<<PAGE 464>>>
Configuring MPLS
Configuring MPLS
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide

page 15-13
Configuring Global LDP Timers
To configure the global LDP timers, use the mpls ldp command. LDP uses the hello messages to establish 
adjacencies with LDP peers. If no hello messages are received from a peer during the hello time that is 
advertised by that peer, the local LDP router will consider the peer as down and will not retain the 
adjacency with that peer.
An interface level hello-interval and keep-alive interval configuration takes precedence over the global 
hello interval and keep-alive interval configuration. Hold time and keep-alive timeout cannot be set to a 
value that is less than three times the hello time and keep-alive interval respectively.
-> mpls ldp hello-interval 10 hold-time 30
-> mpls ldp keepalive-interval 10 keepalive-timeout 30
Configuring LDP Interface
To create MPLS LDP interface and to enable or disable the administrative status of the LDP interface, use 
the mpls ldp interface command. By default, the LDP interface is administratively disabled. 
-> mpls ldp interface vlan10
-> mpls ldp interface admin-state enable
-> mpls ldp interface admin-state disable
On disabling MPLS LDP interface, corresponding LDP interface will be operationally down.
Use the no form of the command to delete the LDP interface.
-> no mpls ldp interface vlan10
Configuring Interface Level LDP Timers
To configure the interface level LDP timers, use the mpls ldp interface command.
The hello interval and keep-alive parameter values configured for an interface takes precedence over the 
global configuration of these values. Hold time and keep-alive timeout cannot be set to a value that is less 
than three times the hello time and keep-alive timeout respectively.
-> mpls ldp interface hello-interval 10 hold-time 30
-> mpls ldp interface keepalive-interval 10 keepalive-timeout 30

<<<PAGE 465>>>
Configuring MPLS
Configuring MPLS
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide

page 15-14
Configuring LDP Graceful Restart
With graceful restart capability enabled, adjacent routers exchange each other's restart capability in their 
initialization messages, and a restart capability per session is established at session startup. 
To enable graceful restart capability of LDP protocol and configure the neighbor liveness and maximum-
recovery timers, use the mpls ldp graceful-restart command. By default, graceful restart along with 
helper mode is enabled.
-> mpls ldp graceful-restart maximum-recovery-time 200 neighbor-liveness-time 
150
Use the no form of this command to disable graceful restart helper of an LDP router.
-> no mpls ldp graceful restart
Enabling or Disabling LDP Session Protection
LDP session protocol feature automatically creates targeted LDP neighborships for all directly connected 
neighbors. When this is enabled, each directly connected neighbor will have two discovery methods, one 
through the dynamic discovery on the interface, and another through the targeted LDP session.
To enable or disable LDP session protection globally, use the mpls ldp session-protection command. 
-> mpls ldp session-protection admin-state enable
-> mpls ldp session-protection admin-state disable
LDP Session Authentication
To maintain integrity of LDP session messages and to prevent introduction of spoofed TCP segments in 
the LDP session connection stream, AOS provides MD5 key based authentication for LDP sessions.
MD5 key (password) for each potential LDP peer on a LDP enabled router can be configured. This key is 
used to compute and append a MD5 signature to each TCP segment carried by the corresponding LDP 
session to that peer. On the receiving end, the MD5 signature is validated to authenticate the peer. 
Authentication must be configured on both LDP peers using the same MD5 key (password), otherwise the 
peer session will not be established.
To set a MD5 password for the TCP session with this LDP peer, use the mpls ldp neighbor command. 
Use the key option to configure MD5 key for the specified LDP peer.
-> mpls ldp neighbor 5.5.5.5 md5 key testkey1
Use the none option to remove the password and disable the session authentication for the LDP peer.
-> mpls ldp neighbor 5.5.5.5 md5 key none

MPLS Ping and Traceroute
MPLS OAM helps service providers monitor Label Switched Paths (LSPs) and quickly isolate MPLS 
forwarding problems to assist with fault detection and troubleshooting in an MPLS network. One of the 
important MPLS OAM features is LSP ping and traceroute, which is used to detect and isolate data plane 
failures in MPLS LSPs when IP reachability and MPLS control plane seem to be working fine.
AOS supports LSP ping and traceroute in accordance with RFC 4379 - Detecting Multi-Protocol Label 
Switched (MPLS) Data Plane Failures.
LSP Ping
MPLS LSP ping uses MPLS echo request and reply packets to validate an LSP. These are analogous to 
Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) echo request and reply messages used to validate reachability 
in IP networks. MPLS OAM echo and reply messages validate data plane reachability in MPLS LDP 
networks. 
MPLS LSP ping function can be used to validate data plane forwarding for IPv4 LDP Forwarding 
Equivalence Classes (FECs). The MPLS echo request packet will be sent to a target router by using the 
label associated with the FEC to be validated. The source address of the LSP echo request is the IP address 
of the LDP router generating the LSP request. The destination IP address will be an address from 
127.x.x.x/8 subnet, which prevents the MPLS echo packets from being IP forwarded and exiting the 
egress provider edge router as an IP packet. 
In response to an MPLS echo request, an MPLS echo reply is sent and forwarded as a non-labeled IP 
packet. The source address of the MPLS echo-reply packet is an address obtained from the router 
generating the echo reply. The destination address is the source address of the router that originated the 
MPLS echo-request packet. The source and destination UDP ports for MPLS echo request and reply 
packets will be 3503.
LSP Traceroute
MPLS LSP traceroute also uses MPLS echo request and reply packets to validate forwarding in a LSP 
hop-by-hop and isolate faults. MPLS LSP traceroute can be used to trace the labeled switched path for a 
LDP IPv4 FEC. 
LSP traceroute uses time-to-live (TTL) field in MPLS to validate the LSP hop-by-hop. When LSP 
traceroute is initiated, it incrementally increases the TTL value in its MPLS echo requests (TTL = 1, 2, 3, 
4) to discover the downstream mapping of each successive hop. The transit router processing the MPLS 
echo request returns an MPLS echo reply containing information about the transit hop in response to the 
TTL-expired MPLS packet.

<<<PAGE 467>>>
Configuring MPLS
MPLS Ping and Traceroute
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide

page 15-16
MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute Operation
Below is an example MPLS LDP topology running IGP (Internal Gateway Protocol) to distribute 
reachability information within the MPLS network.
Figure 15-1 : Example of MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute Operation
LSP ping operation
• When LSP ping is triggered from originating device LER1 for target FEC 2.2.2.2/32, it originates an 
MPLS echo request with target FEC stack TLV having a LDP IPv4 prefix sub-TLV with value 2.2.2.2/
32. LER1 encapsulates the packet with the label assigned to FEC 2.2.2.2/32 and sends it to LSR1.
• LSR1 forwards the MPLS echo request based on the ILM entry in the same way it would forward data 
traffic for FEC 2.2.2.2/32.
• LSR2 receives the MPLS echo request, pops the MPLS label and forwards the packet to LER2 as an IP 
packet.
• LER2 receives the IP packet, processes the MPLS echo request, and sends an MPLS echo reply to 
LER1 as a normal IP packet with return code as 'Replying router is an egress for the FEC'.
• LER1 receives the MPLS echo reply in response to the MPLS echo request and processes it.
LSP traceroute operation
• When LSP traceroute is triggered from originating device LER1 for target FEC 2.2.2.2/32, it originates 
an MPLS echo request with target FEC TLV pointing to 2.2.2.2/32 and downstream mapping TLV 
with NHLFE next hop IP and label. LER1 encapsulates the packet with the label assigned to FEC 
2.2.2.2/32 in NHLFE, set the MPLS TTL value to 1 and sends it to LSR1. 
• LSR1 decrements MPLS TTL and since TTL becomes 0, it processes the echo request. It finds its own 
downstream mapping (ILM entry) based on the incoming label in the request's DS mapping TLV and 
sends an echo reply to LER1 with its own DS mapping TLV.
• LER1 processes the echo reply from LSR1 and then generates another echo request, this time with 
MPLS TTL set to 2.
• LSR1 decrements MPLS TTL and transparently forwards the echo request packet to LSR2 since TTL 
is still non-zero.
• LSR2 decrements MPLS TTL and since TTL becomes 0, it processes the echo request in the same way 
LSR1 had processed.

<<<PAGE 468>>>
Configuring MPLS
MPLS Ping and Traceroute
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 15-17
• LER1 processes the echo reply from LSR2, then generates another echo request, this time with MPLS 
TTL set to 3.
• LSR1 and LSR2 decrement MPLS TTL and transparently forward the echo request packet based on its 
respective ILM entry.
• LER2 receives the echo request, finds that it is the egress router for this FEC and replies with an echo 
reply but without the DS mapping TLV and with return code as ''Replying router is an egress for the 
FEC'.
• LER1 processes the echo reply and since it found the egress LER for the FEC, it completes the 
traceroute process.
Configure MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute
Use mpls ping ldp command to initiate an LSP ping to check the data plane connectivity for MPLS LDP 
LSPs. For example:
-> mpls ping ldp 1.1.1.4/32
Please wait...
Sending 5 MPLS Echos to 1.1.1.4, timeout is 5 seconds
Codes:
'!' - Success, 'Q' - request not sent, '.' - timeout,
'F' No FEC Found, 'R' - Transit (LBL Switched),'X' - Unknown code
Type 'Ctrl+C' to abort

! seq_num = 2 1.1.1.4 0.75 ms
! seq_num = 3 1.1.1.4 0.67 ms
! seq_num = 4 1.1.1.4 0.75 ms
! seq_num = 5 1.1.1.4 0.76 ms

round-trip min/avg/max = 0.67/1.30/1.94

16   Configuring Layer 2 VPN
Services (VPLS, VPWS)
Layer 2 VPNs are a type of Virtual Private Network (VPN) that uses MPLS labels to transport data. The 
communication occurs between routers that are known as Provider Edge routers (PE routers), as they sit on 
the edge of the provider's network, next to the customer's network. L2 VPNs provide multiple types of 
Layer 2 services to the user like Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) that allows E-LAN connectivity 
services over the MPLS network, and VPWS (Virtual Private Wire Service) that provides E-LINE (point 
to point) connectivity.
Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) is a class of VPN service that allows the connection of multiple sites 
in a single bridged domain over a provider-managed IP/MPLS network. The customer sites in a VPLS 
instance appear to be on the same LAN, regardless of their location. VPLS uses an Ethernet interface on 
the customer-facing (access) side, which simplifies the LAN/WAN boundary and allows for rapid and 
flexible service provisioning.
VPWS (Virtual Private Wire Service) is a class of VPN service that provides point-to-point VPN 
connectivity service for customers connected to an MPLS network.
This chapter documents the OmniSwitch implementation of VPLS and VPWS. For information about how 
to configure MPLS, see “Configuring MPLS” chapter in the OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configu-
ration Guide.
In This Chapter
This chapter describes the basic components of VPLS and VPWS and how to configure them through the 
Command Line Interface (CLI). CLI commands are used in the configuration examples; for more details 
about the syntax of commands, see the OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 CLI Reference Guide.

• “Quick Steps for Configuring VPLS” on page 16-4.

Quick Steps for Configuring VPLS
The quick steps described in this section are based on the assumption that an IP/MPLS transport network 
is already in place (see Chapter “Configuring MPLS” for more information).
The following steps provide a quick tutorial for configuring a VPLS service:
1 Setup routing for the interfaces using OSPF. Use the ip interface command to configure the 
Loopback0 interface that will serve as the source IP address of the VPLS gateway (VPLS Tunnel End 
Point). For example:
-> ip interface Loopback0 address 11.255.14.102
2 Load LDP protocol, and enable MPLS and LDP on the interface. An MPLS based network is used as a 
backbone to provide VPN service. VPLS is configured on top of an MPLS based network to setup virtual 
private networks. For example, 
-> mpls load ldp
-> mpls ldp admin-state enable
-> mpls interface vlan_10
-> mpls interface vlan_10 admin-state enable
-> mpls ldp interface vlan_10
-> mpls ldp interface vlan_10 admin-state enable
Refer to the “MPLS Commands” chapter in OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 CLI Reference Guide for more 
information on configuring MPLS and LDP commands and its parameters and usage guidelines.
3 Configure a VPLS service and administratively enable the service using the service vpls command. 
Configure LDP or BGP signaling to establish a pseudowire connection between Provider Edge (PE) rout-
ers. For example:
-> service 1 vpls vplsid 100 signaling ldp description "vpls service with LDP 
signaling" admin-state enable
4 Configure a Service Distribution Point (SDP) for VPLS service, and specify the system (Loopback0) 
IP address of the far-end router using the service sdp mpls command. For example:
-> service sdp 20 mpls far-end 10.10.10.2 description "vpls service with LDP 
signaling" admin-state enable
5
Bind the VPLS service to the SDP tunnel using the service bind-sdp command. For example, the 
following command binds VPLS service 1 to mesh SDP 20:
-> service 1 bind-sdp 20 description "Bind to SDP 20 for service 1"
6 Configure an access port, and configure a Service Access Point (SAP) by associating a VPLS service 
with SAP ID using the service sap command. A SAP ID is comprised of a port or link aggregate and an 
encapsulation value that identifies the device traffic to associate with the service. 
For example, the following command creates a SAP on access port 1/1/1 that will direct customer traffic 
to VPLS service 1:
-> service access port 1/1/1
-> service 1 sap port 1/1/11:100 description “vlan100_sap"
-> service 1 sap port 1/1/11:100 admin-state enable
See “Verifying the VPLS Configuration” on page 16-21 for information about how to display the VPLS 
configuration for the switch.

VPLS Overview
VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service) is a L2VPN technology that allows any to any (multipoint) connec-
tivity. The provider network emulates a LAN by connecting all the customer's remote sites at the edge of 
the provider network to a single bridged LAN. A full mesh of pseudo-wires (PW) needs to be established 
to form a VPLS.
VPLS is a superset of VPWS. VPWS only provides point-to-point customer connectivity without provid-
ing any Layer2 or Layer3 functionality.
A VPLS service-capable network consists of Customer Edges (CE), Provider Edges (PE) and a core 
MPLS network. The CE device is a router or switch located at the customer's premises. It can be owned 
and managed by the customer or owned and managed by the service provider. It is connected to the PE 
through an Attachment Circuit (AC). In the case of VPLS, it is assumed that Ethernet is the layer 2 proto-
col used between the CE and the PE.
The PE device is where the services originate and terminates, and where all the necessary tunnels are set 
up to connect to all the other PEs. As VPLS is an Ethernet layer 2 service, the PE must be capable of 
Media Access Control (MAC) learning, bridging and replication on a per-VPLS basis. The IP/MPLS core 
network interconnects the PEs; it does not really participate in the VPN functionality. Traffic is simply 
switched based on the MPLS labels.
To prevent forwarding loops, the "Split Horizon" rule is used. In the VPLS context, this rule implies that a 
PE must never send a packet on a PW if that packet has been received from a PW. This ensures that traf-
fic cannot form a loop over the backbone network using PWs. The fact that there is always a full mesh of 
PWs between the PE devices ensures that every destination within the VPLS will be reached by a broad-
cast packet.
The following illustration provides an example of an MPLS-based VPLS network:

OmniSwitch implementation of VPLS supports the following:
• VPLS using LDP signaling
• VPLS using BGP for auto-discovery and signaling
VPLS Using LDP Signaling
When you configure VPLS with LDP signaling, LDP supports a full mesh of pseudowires among the 
participating PE routers. 
The three main components of the MPLS based transparent bridging service module are the Service 
Manager, MPLS CMM and the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). The LDP will interface with the IP 
Routing Module (IPRM) to obtain route information that is required to setup label switched paths 
(tunnels). LDP acts as client of the Service Manager. Service Manager requests LDP for initiating and 
managing a tunnel to a far-end termination. LDP is client of MPLS CMM which hosts all the MPLS 
forwarding entries. Service manager interacts with MPLS CMM to obtain transport tunnel labels and also 
the inner labels required for forwarding.

VPLS Using BGP Signaling
The MPLS Layer 2 Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) protocol modules provide transparent LAN 
access between VPN sites. The VPLS BGP Signaling feature enables the auto discovery of PE's or tunnel 
end point in the same VPLS instance.
• Auto-discovery: Discovery refers to the process of finding all the PEs that participate in each VPLS 
instance. A PE either can be configured with the identities of all the other PEs in a given VPLS or can 
use some protocol to discover the other PEs. The latter is called auto- discovery. 
• With auto-discovery, there is no need to configure each VPLS router with all remote endpoints of 
VPLS tunnels, provided there are means to deliver BGP multiprotocol NLRIs between them.
• Signaling: Once discovery is done, each pair of PEs in a VPLS must be able to establish (and tear 
down) pseudowires to each other. This process is known as signaling. MPLS labels exchanged by 
VPLS peers indicate to which specific VPLS a data packet belongs to and also identify the ingress PE 
for the data packet. Using a distinct BGP Update message to send a MPLS label to each remote PE 
would require the originating PE to send N such messages for N remote PEs. There is a solution which 
allows a PE to send a single (common) Update message that contains MPLS labels for all the remote 
PEs, instead of N individual messages.
BGP based VPLS, if configured properly eliminates need to adjust configuration on all routers forming 
VPLS.
BGP VPLS Route Reflection
To reduce the number of BGP peering within an AS is Route Reflection (RR), rather than each BGP 
system having to peer with every other BGP system within the AS, each BGP speaker instead peers with a 
router reflector. Routing advertisements sent to the route reflector are then reflected (sent) out to all of the 
other BGP speakers.
AOS supports BGP Route Reflection for IPv4 and IPv6 Unicast address families. For BGP VPLS route 
reflection, only IPv4 address family is supported. 
If the Route Reflector router itself is configured as a VPLS mesh peer (RR acting as a VPLS PE router) 
for any BGP signaled VPLS service, the normal processing of VPLS NLRI will also be done in addition to 
VPLS NLRI route reflection.
For more information on setting up Route Reflection and Redundant Route Reflectors and its respective 
command parameters and usage guidelines, refer to the “Configuring BGP” and “BGP Commands” 
chapters in the OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide and OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 
CLI Reference Guide.
IPMS L2VPN
The OmniSwitch performs the packet replication required for broadcast and multicast traffic across the 
bridged domain. MAC address learning is performed by the OmniSwitch to reduce the amount of 
unknown destination MAC address flooding.
Each OmniSwitch maintains a Forwarding Information Base (FIB) for each VPLS service instance. 
Source MAC addresses arriving on OmniSwitch access and network ports are learned.and populated in the 
FIB table of the service. 
All traffic is switched based on MAC addresses and forwarded between all participating routers using the 
LSP (Label Switch Path) tunnels. Unknown destination packets are forwarded on all LSPs to the partici-

page 16-8
pating routers for that service until the target station responds and the MAC address is learned by the 
router associated with that service.
VPLS service uses multicast mode as head-end.
Loop Prevention
To prevent forwarding loops, the "Split Horizon" rule is used. In the VPLS context, this rule implies that a 
PE must never send a packet on a pseudowire (PW) if that packet was received from a PW. This ensures 
that traffic cannot form a loop over the backbone network using PWs. 
The fact that there is always a full mesh of PWs between the PE devices ensures that every destination 
within the VPLS will be reached by a broadcast packet.
VPLS Service Components
The OmniSwitch implementation of VPLS is achieved through the Service Manager framework. LANs 
and local devices are associated with a VPLS Service ID through the configuration of service objects. This 
approach requires the configuration of the following service components to define the VPLS service 
domain:
• VPLS Service—The OmniSwitch VPLS gateway identifies each VPLS segment that the gateway 
participates in with a VPLS service ID. A VPLS service is associated with a VPLS Identifier at the 
time the service is created. This type of service represents a single virtual bridge on the gateway 
switch.
• Access Port— A port or link aggregate configured as a service access port. This type of port is 
configured on the VPLS gateway switch to forward traffic to or from the VPLS overlay network. The 
access port is also associated with a Layer 2 profile that specifies how to process protocol control 
frames received on the port.
• Service Access Point (SAP)—A SAP is a logical service entity (also referred to as a virtual port) that 
is configured on a gateway switch to bind an access port and traffic received on that port to a VPLS 
service ID (and the associated VPLS identifier).
• Service Distribution Point (SDP)—An SDP provides a logical point at which device traffic is 
directed from one VPLS gateway to another VPLS gateway. SDPs are used to set up distributed 
services, which consist of at least one SAP on a local node, one SAP on a remote node, and an SDP 
binding the service on both nodes. An SDP serves as the VPLS tunnel interface on a gateway switch.
• SDP Bind—An SDP binding represents the binding of a VPLS service instance to an SDP. The SDP 
then distributes the service connectivity to other VPLS gateways.

Configuring VPLS Services
Configuring a Virtual Private LAN Service requires several steps. These steps are outlined here and 
further described throughout this section. 
1 Configure a VPLS service. Configure service to carry customer traffic through the provider network. 
Configure LDP or BGP signaling to establish a pseudowire connection between Provider Edge (PE) rout-
ers. Subsequently, the service is bound to a SAP to receive customer traffic and bound to a SDP that will 
distribute that traffic through the provider network. See “Configuring VPLS Service” on page 16-10
2 Configure service access ports. One or more access ports are associated with a Service Access Point 
to identify to the service which ports will receive device traffic that the service will process for tunneling 
through the VPLS segment. When an access port is associated with a SAP, the SAP parameter attributes 
are applied to traffic received on the access port. See “Configuring Service Access Ports” on page 16-13.
3 Optionally define access port profile attributes. A default Layer 2 profile is automatically assigned 
to an access port at the time the port is configured as an access port. This profile determines how control 
frames received on the port are processed. It is only necessary to configure a Layer 2 profile if the default 
attribute values are not sufficient. See “Configuring Layer 2 Profiles for Access Ports” on page 16-14.
4 Configure a VPLS Service Access Point (SAP). A SAP binds a VPLS service to an access port and 
defines which device traffic is tunneled through the service. Each SAP is associated to one service ID, but 
a single service can have multiple SAPs to which it is associated. See “Configuring a SAP for VPLS 
Service” on page 16-12.
5 Configure a Service Distribution Point (SDP) for VPLS. A SDP provides a logical service tunnel 
through which traffic is directed from one PE to another PE. Configuring SDPs provides the foundation on 
which services are carried through the IP/MPLS core network. See “Configuring Service Distribution 
Point (SDP) for VPLS” on page 16-19.
6 Bind an SDP tunnel to a VPLS service. Once a VPLS service is created, it is then bound to an SDP. 
See “Binding SDP to a VPLS Service” on page 16-20. This is in case of LDP signaling. If BGP signaling 
is used, dynamic SDP bindings are created.

Configuring VPLS Service
A VPLS service is identified by a service ID number. To configure a VPLS service and administratively 
enable the service, use service vpls command. Use this command to configure signaling to establish a 
pseudowire connection between Provider Edge (PE) routers. Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) / Border 
Gateway Protocol (BGP) can be configured for signaling and to support VPLS auto-discovery between 
VPLS instances.
When VPLS BGP signaling is configured, load BGP protocol using ip load bgp command, enable the 
BGP L2VPN VPLS using the ip bgp address-family l2vpn-vpls command for VPLS BGP route 
exchange. And the respective BGP neighbor must also activate L2VPN VPLS using the ip bgp neighbor 
activate l2vpn-vpls command. Refer to the “BGP Commands” chapter in OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 CLI 
Reference Guide for more information on configuring BGP, BGP peers, and VPLS BGP commands, and 
its parameters and usage guidelines.
Configure an identifier to VPLS Edge (VE) device when BGP is selected as signaling. Each PE device 
participating in a VPLS must have at least one VE ID. The valid range 1–1000. This should be unique 
among the VPLS peers for a VPLS instance.
Optionally, specify the Maximum Transfer Unit (MTU) size for the VPLS service during signaling using 
the service-mtu parameter.
For example:
-> service 1 vpls vplsid 100 signaling ldp description "vpls service instance 
100" service-mtu 9000 admin-state enable
-> service 2 vpls vplsid 200 signaling bgp ve-id 1 admin-state enable
To remove a VPLS service, administratively disable the service, then use the no form of this command 
and specify the service ID of the disabled service.
-> no service 1 vpls

The following VPLS service parameter values are set by default at the time the service is created. If 
necessary, use the specified commands to change the default values.

Using VLAN Translation
VLAN translation refers to the egress translation of VLAN tags on service access points (SAPs). When 
enabled for a service, the VLAN tags for outgoing VM frames on SAPs associated with that service are 
processed according to the local SAP configuration (the SAP on which the frames will egress) and not 
according to the configuration of the SAP on which the frames were received.

• If the local SAP is configured for untagged traffic (chassis/slot/port:0), the egress traffic is always sent 
out as untagged.
• If the local SAP is configured for 802.1q-tagged traffic (chassis/slot/port:ctag), the egress traffic is 
single-tagged with the tag value specified by the ctag (customer VLAN tag) value.
• If the local SAP is configured for double-tagged traffic (chassis/slot/port:outer_tag.: inner_tag), the 
egress traffic is double-tagged with the tag values specified by the outer_tag and inner_tag values.
When VLAN translation is disabled, frames simply egress without any modification of the VLAN tags. In 
other words, the frames are transparently bridged without tag modification.
The following table shows the required translation (tag is added or replaced) that takes place when the 
egress SAP configuration is applied to the possible frame types (untagged, tagged, double-tagged). Note 
that in this table the terms “ITAG” and “OTAG” refer to inner tag and outer tag, respectively.
Enabling VLAN translation is required at two different levels: first at the access port level and then at the 
service level. This activates VPLS translation for all of the SAPs on an access port that belong to the same 
service.
To enable translation at the service level, use the service vlan-xlation command. For example:
-> service 10 vlan-xlation enable
To enable VLAN translation for all services, use the all parameter with the same command. For example:
-> service all vlan-xlation enable
To disable VLAN translation, use the service vlan-xlation command with the disable parameter. For 
example:
-> service 10 vlan-xlation disable
-> service all vlan-xlation disable
To enable VLAN translation at the port level, use the service access vlan-xlation command. For example:
-> service access port 1/1/1 vlan-xlation enable
See “Configuring Service Access Ports” on page 16-13 for more information.

Enable/Disable a VPLS Service
Once the service is created and any optional service parameters are configured, use the service admin-
state command with the enable option to enable the service. By default, the VPLS service is enabled 
when the service is created.
For example:
-> service 10 admin-state enable
To disable the service, enter the following command:
-> service 10 admin-state disable
Configuring a SAP for VPLS Service
A SAP identifies the location where customer traffic enters the provider network edge, the type of 
customer traffic to service, parameters to apply to the traffic, and the service that will process the traffic 
for tunneling through the provider network.
Configuring a SAP requires several steps. 
• Configure customer-facing ports or link aggregates as service access ports. 
• Configure the access port encapsulation mode to determine if the port will support a single SAP (one 
customer service) or multiple SAPs (customer services). 
• Configure Layer 2 profiles to determine how control packets are processed on access ports.
• Create a SAP by associating a SAP ID with a VPLS service ID. A SAP ID is comprised of an access 
port and an encapsulation value, which is used to identify the type of customer traffic to map to the 
associated service.
Configure an access port, and configure a Service Access Point (SAP) by associating a SAP ID with 
VPLS service using the service sap command. For example, the following command creates a SAP on 
access port 1/1/1 that will direct customer traffic to VPLS service 1:
-> service access port 1/1/1
-> service 1 sap port 1/1/2:0

Service Access Port Configuration Guidelines
Consider the following when configuring a SAP (Service Access Port):
• A SAP is a unique local entity for any given device. The same SAP ID value can be used on other 
VPLS gateway switches. 
• There are no SAPs configured by default; explicit configuration of a SAP is required.
• A SAP is administratively enabled at the time the SAP is created.
• When a SAP is deleted, all configuration parameters for the SAP are also deleted.
• A SAP is owned by and associated with the service that was specified at the time the SAP was created. 
• Multiple SAPs with different service types, such as a VPLS, VXLAN, or SPB service are allowed on 
the same service access port.
• If a port is administratively shutdown, all SAPs on that port become operationally out of service.
• Both fixed ports and link aggregates are configurable as access ports. Only access ports are associated 
with SAPs.
• Bridging functionality is not supported on access ports or link aggregates.
• Configuring multiple SAPs on an access port that map different VLAN tags to the same service can 
cause a MAC move when the same MAC address ingresses the access port with different VLAN tags. 
For example, a MAC has two flows tagged with VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 that ingress access port 1/1/1 
and both flows are mapped to service 100. 
-> service 100 sap port 1/1/1:10
-> service 100 sap port 1/1/1:20
To avoid the MAC move in this scenario, use one of the following alternative SAP configurations.
Configure the SAPs with different services:
-> service 100 sap port 1/1/1:10
-> service 200 sap port 1/1/1:20
Configure a default SAP to classify both flows into the same service:
-> service 100 sap port 1/1/1:all
See “Creating the Service Access Point” on page 16-16 for more information.
Configuring Service Access Ports
Each SAP is comprised of a service access port or link aggregate and an encapsulation type value. Access 
ports are configured on a VPLS gateway switch to forward traffic to or from a VPLS segment. Traffic 
received on these ports is classified for one or more SAPs and forwarded onto the intended destination by 
the associated VPLS service.
To configure a port or link aggregate as an access port, use the service access command. For example, the 
following command configures port 1/1/2 and link aggregate 100 as access ports:
-> service access port 1/1/2
-> service access linkagg 100 description "Server Access Port"

In the link aggregate example, an optional description parameter is used to add information to the access 
port. This parameter is available at the time the port is configured as an access port or to change or remove 
a description from an existing access port. For example, the following command removes the description 
from link aggregate 100:
-> service access linkagg 100 no description "Server Access Port"
After the description is removed, link aggregate 100 continues to operate as a service access port. To 
revert an access port back to a regular switch port or link aggregate, use the no form of the service access 
command. For example:
-> no service access port 1/1/2
-> no service access linkagg 100
VLAN Translation on Access Ports
VLAN translation refers to the egress translation of VLAN tags on service access points (SAPs). For more 
information about how VLAN translation is applied, see “Using VLAN Translation” on page 16-10. 
By default, VLAN translation is disabled on access ports. Enabling VLAN translation on an access port 
implicitly enables translation for all SAPs associated with that port. However, translation must also be 
enabled for the services associated with these SAPs. This ensures that all SAPs associated with a service 
will apply VLAN translation.
To enable VLAN translation on an access port, use the service access vlan-xlation command with the 
enable option. For example:
-> service access port 1/1/3 vlan-xlation enable
-> service access linkagg 10 vlan-xlation enable
To disable VLAN translation on an access port, use the service access vlan-xlation command with the 
disable option. For example:
-> service access port 1/1/3 vlan-xlation disable
-> service access linkagg 10 vlan-xlation disable

A Layer 2 profile determines how ingress control frames on an access port are processed. When a port is 
configured as an access port, a default Layer 2 profile (def-access-profile) is applied to the port with the 
following default values for processing control frames:

Consider the following when configuring Layer 2 profiles:
• Not all of the control protocols are currently supported with the peer, tunnel, and discard parameters. 
Use the following table to determine the parameter combinations that are supported: 
• When a profile is created, the new profile inherits the default profile settings for processing control

To delete a Layer 2 profile, use the no form of the service l2profile command. For example, the following

Assigning Layer 2 Profiles to Access Ports
After a Layer 2 profile is created, it is then necessary to assign the profile to an access port or link 
aggregate. When this is done, the current profile associated with the port is replaced with the new profile. 
The service access l2profile command is used to assign a new profile to an access port. For example, the 
following command assigns the “DropL2” profile to access port 1/1/4:
-> service access port 1/1/4 l2profile DropL2
-> service access linkagg 5 l2profile DropL2
To change the profile associated with the access port back to the default profile (def-access-profile), use 
the default option with the service access l2profile command. For example:
-> service access port 1/1/4 l2profile default
-> service access linkagg 5 l2profile DropL2
Use the show service access command to display profile associations for access ports.
Creating the Service Access Point
Each VPLS service is bound to at least one Service Access Point (SAP). A SAP identifies the point at 
which traffic enters the VPLS segment. A SAP is one of the required service components that is needed to 
designate an OmniSwitch as a VPLS gateway device. 
A SAP is created by associating a SAP ID with a VPLS service. A SAP ID is comprised of an access port 
and an encapsulation value that is used to identify the type of device traffic (untagged, single-tagged, or 
double-tagged) to map to the associated service. 
The service sap command is used to configure a SAP. This command specifies the VPLS service ID 
number and the SAP ID (slot/port:encapsulation). The following parameter values are used with this 
command to specify the encapsulation value:
*Note that the :all (wildcard) parameter is also configurable as the inner tag value for double-tagged 
frames (for example, “10:all” specifies double-tagged packets with an outer tag equal to 10 and an 
inner tag with any value).
The following service sap command example creates a SAP that will direct ingress traffic on access port 
1/4 that is tagged with VLAN ID 50 to service 100:
-> service 100 sap port 1/1/1:50 description “Server1 to VPLS SAP”
In the above example, the 1/1/1:50 designation is referred to as the SAP ID or the encapsulation ID. This 
means that if no other SAPs are configured for port 1/1/1, then any ingress traffic on that port is dropped if 
the traffic is not tagged with VLAN 50.

all

classified into another SAP*
qtag

VLAN ID.
outer_qtag.innger_qtag

Configuring Multiple SAPs on the Same Access Port
It is possible to configure more than one SAP for the same access port, which provides a method for 
segregating incoming traffic into multiple services. For example, the following SAP configuration for port 
2/3 sends incoming traffic to three different services based on the VLAN tags of the frames received:
-> service 2000 sap port 1/2/3:all
-> service 200 sap port 1/2/3:100
-> service 1000 sap port 1/2/3:100.200
In this example,
• Frames double-tagged with 100 (outer tag) and 200 (inner tag) are sent on service 1000.
• Frames single-tagged with VLAN 100 are sent on service 200.
• All other frames (those that are not single-tagged with 100 or double-tagged with 100 and 200) are sent 
on service 2000.
The following SAP ID classification precedence is applied when there are multiple SAPs for one access 
port:
1 Double-tagged (Outer VLAN + Inner VLAN) - Highest 
2 Double-tagged (Outer VLAN + all)
3 Single-tagged (VLAN)
4 Single-tagged (wildcard)
5 Untagged - Lowest.
Configuring a Range of Ports or VLAN IDs for the SAP ID
It is possible to specify a range of service access ports or a range of VLAN IDs when configuring a SAP. 
For example, the following command configures a range of access ports and VLAN IDs for the SAP ID:
-> service 10 sap port 1/1/11-20:21-30 description "SAPs on ports 1/1/11 to 1/1/
20 with tag 21 to 30"
In this example, any ingress traffic on access ports 1/1/11 through 1/1/20 that is tagged with a VLAN ID 
in the range of 21 through 30 is classified into the VPLS SAP. The following command provides an 
example of specifying a range of link aggregate access ports:
-> service 20 sap linkagg 1-10:100 un-trusted description “Untrusted SAPs for 
lag 1-10 with tag 100"

The following parameter values are set by default at the time the SAP is created. If necessary, use the 
specified commands to change the default values.

service sap trusted

Refer to the OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 CLI Reference Guide for more information about the command 
parameters.
Configuring the SAP Trust Mode
The service sap trusted command is used to configure the trust mode for a SAP. A trusted SAP can 
accept 802.1p values in incoming packets; an untrusted SAP will set any 802.1p values to zero in the 
incoming packets, unless an 802.1p value is configured with this command.
Note that untagged Layer 2 control packets (for example, BPDU, GVRP, and AMAP) are always tunneled 
(if enabled) through the VPLS segment with the default EXP bits set to 7, so that they can arrive at the 
destination bridge at the highest COS queue of 7. As a result, trusted and untrusted SAPs configured on 
the access ports will not affect the Layer 2 control packets received on the access ports.
By default, a SAP is trusted with the priority set to best effort (zero). Use the service sap trusted 
command with the un-trusted and priority options to change the SAP mode to untrusted. For example: 
-> service 100 sap 1/1/4:50 untrusted priority 7
When a SAP is trusted, the priority value contained in tagged device packets is used; untagged packets are 
assigned the default priority value (zero). When a SAP is untrusted, the priority value configured for the 
SAP is assigned to both tagged and untagged customer packets.
Enabling/Disabling the SAP
By default, a SAP is enabled at the time the SAP is created. To disable the SAP administrative status, use 
the service sap admin-state command. For example:
-> service 100 sap port 1/1/4:50 admin-state disable
-> service 200 sap linkagg 5:all admin-state disable
To enable the SAP, enter the following command:
-> service 100 sap port 1/1/4:50 admin-state enable
-> service 200 sap linkagg 5:all admin-state enable
Deleting the SAP
When a SAP is administratively disabled, the SAP configuration is not removed from the switch. To 
delete a SAP from the switch configuration, use the no form of the service sap command. For example:
-> no service 100 sap port 1/1/4:50
-> no service 200 sap linkagg 5:all
Verifying the SAP Configuration
A SAP is a type of virtual port that is associated with a VPLS service. To determine the SAP configuration 
for a specific service, use the show service ports command to view the virtual ports associated with a 
specific service. To view the configuration information for a specific VPLS network identifier, use the 
show service ports command with the vpls parameter option. 
For example:
-> show service vpls 100 ports

Configuring Service Distribution Point (SDP) for VPLS
Consider the following when configuring SDPs when VPLS LDP signaling is configured.
• A SDP is identified by an ID number. This ID number is used to bind the SDP to a service and LSPs
• The SDP uses the system (Loopback0) IP address to identify the far-end router.
• Each router must have an SDP defined for every remote router to which the local router will provide 
service. In addition, a return path SDP is required from every remote router to the local router, as SDP 
tunnels are uni-directional.
• More than one SDP to the same far-end router is allowed as long as each SDP uses a different type of 
transport.
• A VPLS service requires an SDP binding. By default, no SDP is associated with a VPLS service. The 
SDP is created first and then bound to the VPLS service.
• An SDP is not specific or exclusive to any one service or any type of service. An SDP can have more 
than one service binding. However, any administrative or operational activity that occurs on the SDP 
affects all the services associated with that SDP.
To configure a SDP for VPLS service, specify the system (Loopback0) IP address of the far-end router, 
and administratively enable SDP using the service sdp mpls command. For example:
-> service sdp 20 mpls far-end 10.10.10.2 description "vpls service with LDP 
signaling" admin-state enable
The far-end IP address value specifies a single destination unicast IP address that identifies the far-end 
VPLS tunnel access switch to which the SDP will tunnel traffic. 
Note that once a far-end address is specified for the SDP, a service tunnel instance is created between the 
local and the remote routers. A return SDP tunnel is required from the remote router to the local router, as 
SDP tunnels are uni-directional.
Use the no form of this command to delete the SDP object, only if the SDP is not bound to any services. If 
the description parameter is specified with the no form, then only the description information is removed 
from the SDP. For example:
-> no service sdp 20

Enabling or Disabling an SDP
By default, an SDP is enabled at the time the SDP is created. To disable the SDP administrative status, use 
the service sdp command with the admin-state parameter option. For example:
-> service sdp 10 admin-state disable
-> service sdp 20 admin-state disable
To enable an SDP, enter the following commands:
-> service sdp 10 admin-state enable
-> service sdp 20 admin-state enable
Deleting an SDP
When an SDP is administratively disabled, the SDP configuration is not removed from the switch. To 
delete an SDP from the switch configuration, use the no form of the service sdp command. For example:
-> no service sdp 10
-> no service sdp 20
Binding SDP to a VPLS Service
A mesh-SDP binding with a service is logically treated as a single bridge port for flooded traffic, where 
flooded traffic received on any mesh SDP for the service is replicated to other ports and not transmitted on 
any mesh SDPs.
Binding an SDP to a VPLS instance is required to set up a Virtual Circuit (VC)/Pseudo Wire (PW) to the 
far end of the MPLS tunnel. If an SDP is not explicitly bound to a service, no far-end routers can partici-
pate in the service.
To configure a mesh-SDP binding, use the service bind-sdp command. For example, the following 
command binds VPLS service 1 to mesh SDP 20:
-> service 1 bind-sdp 20 description "Bind to SDP 20 for service 1"

Verifying the VPLS Configuration
A summary of the commands used for verifying the VPLS configuration is given here: 
For more information about the output details that result from these commands, see the OmniSwitch AOS 
Release 8 CLI Reference Guide.
show service
Displays information about the VPLS service configured on the 
switch.
show service ports
Displays the virtual ports associated with the specified VPLS 
service. 
show service vpls sap
Displays the configuration information for the specified Service 
Access Point (SAP) ID associated with the specified VPLS service.
show service debug-info
Displays debug information for the virtual ports associated with the 
VPLS service.
show service info
Displays the Service Manager configuration for the local switch.
show service sdp mpls
Displays the SDP configuration for VPLS services. 
show service bind-sdp vpls
Displays the SDP binding configuration for VPLS services. 
show service mesh-sdp
Displays the bindings between VPLS service and SDPs. 
show service vpls mesh-sdp
Displays SDP bindings with the specified SDP ID and/or service ID 
number.

Quick Steps for Configuring VPWS
The quick steps described in this section are based on the assumption that an IP/MPLS transport network 
is already in place (see Chapter “Configuring MPLS” for more information).
The following steps provide a quick tutorial for configuring a VPWS service:
1 Setup routing for the interfaces using OSPF. Use the ip interface command to configure the 
Loopback0 interface that will serve as the source IP address of the VPWS gateway (VPWS Tunnel End 
Point). For example:
-> ip interface Loopback0 address 11.255.10.102
2 Load LDP protocol, and enable MPLS and LDP on the interface. An MPLS based network is used as a 
backbone to provide VPN service. VPWS is configured on top of an MPLS based network to setup virtual 
private networks. For example, 
-> mpls load ldp
-> mpls ldp admin-state enable
-> mpls interface vlan_10
-> mpls interface vlan_10 admin-state enable
-> mpls ldp interface vlan_10
-> mpls ldp interface vlan_10 admin-state enable
Refer to the “MPLS Commands” chapter in OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 CLI Reference Guide for more 
information on configuring MPLS and LDP commands and its parameters and usage guidelines.
3 Configure a VPWS service and administratively enable the service using the service vpws command. 
For example:
-> service 2 vpws vcid 200 description "VPWS test svc" admin-state enable
4 Configure a Service Distribution Point (SDP) for VPWS service, and specify the system (Loopback0) 
IP address of the far-end router using the service sdp mpls command. For example:
-> service sdp 30 mpls far-end 9.1.1.3 description "VPWS Peer"
5
Bind the VPWS service to the SDP tunnel using the service bind-sdp command. Specify the ‘spoke’ 
option when binding a SDP to a VPWS service. For example, the following command binds VPWS 
service 1 to mesh SDP 20:
-> service 2 bind-sdp 20 spoke description "Bind SDP to VPWS service"
6 Configure an access port, and configure a Service Access Point (SAP) by associating a VPWS service 
with SAP ID using the service sap command. A SAP ID is comprised of a port or link aggregate and an 
encapsulation value that identifies the device traffic to associate with the service. 
For example, the following command creates a SAP on access port 1/1/1 that will direct customer traffic 
to VPWS service 2:
-> service access port 1/1/1
-> service 2 sap port 1/1/11:100 description “vlan100_sap"
-> service 2 sap port 1/1/11:100 admin-state enable

<<<PAGE 507>>>

Quick Steps for Configuring VPWS

page 16-34
7 Use the ip interface command to configure the Loopback0 interface that will serve as the source IP 
address of the VPWS gateway (VPWS Tunnel End Point). 
-> ip interface Loopback0 address 11.255.14.102
See “Verifying the VPWS Configuration” on page 16-49 for information about how to display the VPWS 
configuration for the switch.

Configuring Layer 2 VPN Services (VPLS, VPWS)
VPWS Overview
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide

VPWS Overview
VPWS (Virtual Private Wire Service) provides P2P (Point-to-Point) VPN connectivity service for 
customers connected to an MPLS network.
Based on MPLS technology, VPWS allows multiple customers to share one transport leased line (LSP- 
Label Switch Path) and create an exclusive virtual channel for each customer on the shared LSP. On an 
Ethernet network, sites in different cities can communicate over a P2P VPWS connection on an MPLS 
network, just like communicating within a VLAN.
The basic VPWS architecture consists of three components: Attachment Circuits (AC) also referred to as 
SAPs (Service Access Points), VC (Virtual Circuits) and tunnels. PW (Pseudo Wire) is also a common 
term used to specify a VPWS service. Figure below shows the basic VPWS architecture.
Figure 16-1 : MPLS Based VPWS Network
• Attachment Circuit or SAP - It is a connection between the customer equipment (CE) and the provider 
edge (PE) device, called the CE-PE link. A SAP can be a physical interface or a virtual interface 
(VLAN based). 
• Virtual Circuit - A unidirectional logical connection between two PE devices per VPWS service. The 
VC ID identifies a VC. VCs must have unique IDs on a PE.
• Tunnel - A virtual link that transparently carries traffic of one or more VPWS services. With MPLS as 
transport, the tunnel is a LSP between the two endpoints (PEs) of the P2P VPWS service.
To establish a VPWS service, it is required to establish a VC and tunnel, and then bind the SAP to the VC. 
Once the VPWS service is established, L2VPN traffic can flow between CEs in two customer VPN sites 
as if they were in the same Virtual-LAN in the same premises. 
The below sequence describes the data traffic flow from CE1 and CE3 in VPN1 in the reference diagram 
shown above:

<<<PAGE 509>>>
Configuring Layer 2 VPN Services (VPLS, VPWS)
VPWS Overview
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 16-36
• CE1 sends user (L2VPN) packets to the PE over an AC (SAP).
• Upon receipt, PE1 selects a Virtual Circuit or PW to forward the packets based on the SAP 
configuration and ingress outer VLAN tag.
• PE1 adds double MPLS labels (one VC label and one tunnel label) to the packet according to the 
VPWS forwarding entry. The VC label identifies the VPWS service (PW) and the tunnel label 
identifies the public network LSP used to transport L2VPN user data.
• After user packets travel along the public MPLS cloud to PE2, PE2 extracts the VC label. The tunnel 
label is extracted by means of penultimate hop popping (PHP) on the penultimate LSR router.
• PE2 then selects the Attachment Circuit based on the VC to SAP mapping table and forwards the 
packets to CE3.
VPWS, unlike VPLS, does not learn MAC addresses on SAP or SDP port and does not need to enable 
MAC learning. This makes it a very appealing service in traditional leased line applications. VPLS is by 
default a full-mesh topology, so even if used for P2P L2VPN application, this service inherently emulates 
an Ethernet switch and requires flooding and source MAC address learning to make forwarding decisions. 
LDP is used as the signaling protocol to transmit VC related information between the local and remote 
peer for VPWS services. AOS will only support LDP based VPWS services.
VPWS Service Components
The OmniSwitch implementation of VPWS is achieved through the Service Manager framework. LANs 
and local devices are associated with a VPWS Service ID through the configuration of service objects. 
This approach requires the configuration of the following service components to define the VPWS service 
domain:
• VPWS service: The OmniSwitch VPWS gateway identifies each VPWS segment that the gateway 
participates in with a VPWS service ID. A VPWS service is associated with a VPWS Identifier at the 
time the service is created. This type of service represents a single virtual bridge on the gateway 
switch.
• Access Port. A port or link aggregate configured as a service access port. This type of port is 
configured on the VPWS gateway switch to forward traffic to or from the VPWS overlay network. The 
access port is also associated with a Layer 2 profile that specifies how to process protocol control 
frames received on the port.
• Service Access Point (SAP)—A SAP is a logical service entity (also referred to as a virtual port) that 
is configured on a gateway switch to bind an access port and traffic received on that port to a VPWS 
service ID (and the associated VPWS identifier).
• Service Distribution Point (SDP)—An SDP provides a logical point at which device traffic is 
directed from one VPWS gateway to another VPWS gateway. SDPs are used to set up distributed 
services, which consist of at least one SAP on a local node, one SAP on a remote node, and an SDP 
binding the service on both nodes. An SDP serves as the VPWS tunnel interface on a gateway switch.
• SDP Bind—An SDP binding represents the binding of a VPWS service instance to an SDP. The SDP 
then distributes the service connectivity to other VPWS gateways.

<<<PAGE 510>>>
Configuring Layer 2 VPN Services (VPLS, VPWS)
Configuring VPWS Services
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 16-37
Configuring VPWS Services
Configuring a Virtual Private Wire Service requires several steps. These steps are outlined here and 
further described throughout this section. 
1 Configure a VPWS service. Configure service to carry customer traffic through the provider network. 
Subsequently, the service is bound to a SAP to receive customer traffic and bound to a SDP that will 
distribute that traffic through the provider network. See “Configuring VPWS Service” on page 16-38
2 Configure service access ports. One or more access ports are associated with a Service Access Point 
to identify to the service which ports will receive device traffic that the service will process for tunneling 
through the VPWS segment. When an access port is associated with a SAP, the SAP parameter attributes 
are applied to traffic received on the access port. See “Configuring Service Access Ports” on page 16-13.
3 Optionally define access port profile attributes. A default Layer 2 profile is automatically assigned 
to an access port at the time the port is configured as an access port. This profile determines how control 
frames received on the port are processed. It is only necessary to configure a Layer 2 profile if the default 
attribute values are not sufficient. See “Configuring Layer 2 Profiles for Access Ports” on page 16-14.
4 Configure a VPWS Service Access Point (SAP). A SAP binds a VPWS service to an access port and 
defines which device traffic is tunneled through the service. Each SAP is associated to one service ID, but 
a single service can have multiple SAPs to which it is associated. See “Configuring a SAP for VPWS 
Service” on page 16-40.
5 Configure a Service Distribution Point (SDP) for VPWS. A SDP provides a logical service tunnel 
through which traffic is directed from one PE to another PE. Configuring SDPs provides the foundation on 
which services are carried through the IP/MPLS core network. See “Configuring Service Distribution 
Point (SDP) for VPWS” on page 16-47.
6 Bind an SDP tunnel to a VPWS service. Once a VPWS service is created, it is then bound to an SDP. 
See “Binding SDP to a VPWS Service” on page 16-48.

Configuring VPWS Service
A VPWS service is identified by a service ID number. To configure a VPWS service and administratively 
enable the service, use service vpws command.
For example:
-> service 2 vpws vcid 200 description "VPWS test svc" admin-state enable
-> service 2 vpws vcid 200 admin-state enable
To remove a VPWS service, administratively disable the service, then use the no form of this command 
and specify the service ID of the disabled service.
-> no service 2 vpws
Modifying Default VPWS Service Parameters
The following VPWS service parameter values are set by default at the time the service is created. If 
necessary, use the specified commands to change the default values.
Refer to the OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 CLI Reference Guide for more information about the above 
parameters and related commands.
Using VLAN Translation
VLAN translation refers to the egress translation of VLAN tags on service access points (SAPs). When 
enabled for a service, the VLAN tags for outgoing VM frames on SAPs associated with that service are 
processed according to the local SAP configuration (the SAP on which the frames will egress) and not 
according to the configuration of the SAP on which the frames were received.
• If the local SAP is configured for untagged traffic (slot/port:0), the egress traffic is always sent out as 
untagged.
• If the local SAP is configured for 802.1q-tagged traffic (slot/port:ctag), the egress traffic is single-
tagged with the tag value specified by the ctag (customer VLAN tag) value.
• If the local SAP is configured for double-tagged traffic (slot/port:outer_tag.: inner_tag), the egress 
traffic is double-tagged with the tag values specified by the outer_tag and inner_tag values.
When VLAN translation is disabled, frames simply egress without any modification of the VLAN tags. In 
other words, the frames are transparently bridged without tag modification.

that in this table the terms “ITAG” and “OTAG” refer to inner tag and outer tag, respectively.
Enabling VLAN translation is required at two different levels: first at the access port level and then at the 
service level. This activates VPWS translation for all of the SAPs on an access port that belong to the 
same service.
To enable translation at the service level, use the service vlan-xlation command. For example:
-> service 10 vlan-xlation enable
To enable VLAN translation for all services, use the all parameter with the same command. For example:
-> service all vlan-xlation enable
To disable VLAN translation, use the service vlan-xlation command with the disable parameter. For 
example:
-> service 10 vlan-xlation disable
-> service all vlan-xlation disable
To enable VLAN translation at the port level, use the service access vlan-xlation command. For example:
-> service access port 1/1/1 vlan-xlation enable
