Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
EVPN Overview
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-5
EVPN Overview
Ethernet VPN (EVPN) is an extension to the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). It allows the network to 
carry endpoint reachability information, such as Layer 2 MAC addresses and Layer 3 IP addresses. EVPN 
provides multi-path forwarding and redundancy through an all-active multihoming model. Multihoming 
allows to connect a host to more than one network. Connecting to multiple networks can increase 
reliability because if one connection fails, packets can still be routed through the remaining connection. It 
also helps to avoid flooding in the Layer 2 network.
In AOS, the EVPN protocol is based on the MP-BGP and provides additional support to the existing AOS 
overlay services. The EVPN based services provide multihoming capability for the access host devices 
along with the L2 and L3 mobility for the connected hosts. The multihoming of the hosts will provide 
better network utilization due to the multi-path routes and provide network redundancy for the hosts. The 
EVPN based networks also reduces the amount of broadcast traffic in the overlay network. This is 
achieved by managing the L2 and L3 host FDB entries in the control plane. In Layer 2 networks, the 
reachability information is distributed in the data plane by flooding. Since the MAC learning is handled in 
the control plane with EVPN architecture, it avoids the flooding in Layer 2 by advertising the MAC 
address to the interested parties.
EVPN Components
EVPN comprises of the various devices and Layer 2/Layer 3 functionalities:
VLAN: The Virtual Area Network (VLAN) identifies a VLAN group and maintains the information 
related to the users or host connected to the VLAN.
CE: Customer Edge devices (CE) is a layer 2 switch or router which provides access to the connected PE 
(Provider Edge) devices.
PE: Provider Edge devices (PE) connects different network sites using the EVPN. They enable layer 2 
virtual connectivity between the CE devices.
EVI: Ethernet VPN Instance (EVI) is a EVPN forwarding and routing instance, which spans across all the 
PE devices in the EVPN network. It is configured per-customer basis and consists of Route Distinguisher 
(RD) and Route Target (RT).
ES: Ethernet Segment (ES) is a set of Ethernet link connecting a group of PEs.
ESI: Ethernet Segment Identifier/Index (ESI) is a 10-byte unique nonzero identifier used to identify an ES 
(Example: 03:22:33:44:55:66:77:88:99). The ESI is required by the multihoming CEs for the linking. In 
case of ALE, Singlehomed devices also use the nonzero identifier. This gives a leverage to use all the 
advantages of ESI for Singlehoming. This is interoperable with other external implementations.
VTEP: VXLAN Tunnel End Point (VTEP), which handles the traffic forwarding between different 
VXLAN networks.
MP-BGP: Multiprotocol Border Gateway Protocol (MP-BGP) is the main signaling protocol used by 
EVPN.
EVPN Address Family: It defines the type of BGP EVPN routes.
DF: The Designated Forwarder plays a crucial role in managing the forwarding of multicast, broadcast, 
and unknown unicast (BUM) traffic within an EVPN network, particularly in scenarios involving 
multi-homed Ethernet segments.

<<<PAGE 584>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
EVPN Overview
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-6
NDF: The Non-Designated Forwarder role complements the Designated Forwarder (DF) in managing 
Ethernet segments, especially in multi-homed scenarios. Non-Designated Forwarders are the PE devices 
that are part of the multi-homed Ethernet segment but are not elected as the DF. NDFs do not forward 
BUM traffic for the Ethernet segment. This responsibility is exclusive to the DF to ensure a loop-free 
environment.
RT-1A (Ethernet Segment Route): This is used to advertise the presence of an Ethernet segment and 
includes information necessary for Designated Forwarder (DF) election.
RT-1B (Ethernet Auto-Discovery Route): This is used to advertise auto-discovery information for a 
particular Ethernet segment and enables the identification of all PEs connected to that segment.
EVPN Route Types: EVPN uses the following route types to advertise. They are:
–
Type 1: Ethernet Auto Discovery (AD) Route
–
Type 2: Host Advertisement Route
–
Type 3: Inclusive Multicast Route
–
Type 4: Ethernet Segment Route
–
Type 6: Selective Multicast Ethernet Tag Route
–
Type 7: Multicast Membership Report Synch Route
–
Type 8: Multicast Leave Synch Route
BGP EVPN Route Types
The EVPN protocol operation is best described by expanding on the functional behavior for each Route 
Type. The PE (Provider Edge) is identified by the Loopback0 IP address used by BGP to setup the peer 
sessions.
The BGP EVPN protocol is supported by using the BGP route types (Type 1 to Type 8) to orchestrate the 
EVPN functionality. Each route type has a specific function in the operation of an overlay EVPN network 
as listed:
Type 1: Ethernet Auto Discovery (AD) Route
It is advertised by the PE that is part of the CE device (singlehomed/multihomed). The Ethernet AD routes 
are of two types:
• AD route per ESI: It is used for mass convergence, mass withdraw, link failure, and split horizon filter 
for multihoming.
• AD route per EVI: It is used to enable active-active load balancing to PEs connected to multihoming 
CEs.
Type 2: Host Advertisement Route
It is used to advertise the reachability of the MAC address in the EVPN network.
Type 3: Inclusive Multicast Route
This allows ingress replication for forwarding Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, and Multicast (BUM) traffic 
between PEs across EVPN network.
Type 4: Ethernet Segment Route
It is used to advertise between PEs connected to multi-homed CEs in the same ESI. It is also used in 
Designated Forwarder (DF) election process, which is used to send BUM traffic.

<<<PAGE 585>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
EVPN Overview
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-7
Type 5: IP Prefix Route
Supports overlay L3VPN operation. And, It is used to advertise the prefix routes associated with an 
overlay VPN interface.
Type 6: Selective Multicast Ethernet Tag Route
Support for IGMP and MLD proxy functionality for single homed and multihomed CE nodes.
Type 7: Multicast Membership Report Synch Route
This route type is used to coordinate the IGMP Membership Report (x,G) state for a given BD between 
the PEs attached to a given ES operating in All-Active (or Single-Active) redundancy mode.
Type 8: Multicast Leave Synch Route
This EVPN route type is used to coordinate the IGMP Leave Group (x,G) state for a given BD between 
the PEs attached to a given ES operating in an All-Active (or Single-Active) redundancy mode.

OmniSwitch EVPN Service Model
The AOS EVPN service model provides enhanced stability, better scalability, and improved convergence 
of BGP based EVPN network by:
• Instantiating an ES Index (ESI) for any access port that is enabled for EVPN. This allows the access 
port types (physical, single-homed (SH) or linkagg/multi-homed (MH) ports) to work efficiently by 
using the EVPN control plane based Forwarding Database management.
• Enabling deployment of AOS EVPN on both Enterprise and Data-Center network due to the capability 
of associating ESIs for all access port types.
• Providing high granularity, by generating the ESI+ETag aware routes.
OmniSwitch EVPN ESI Model
The AOS EVPN model allows to generate the ESI value automatically and manually. The AOS EVPN 
model automates the ESI generation wherever possible to simplify the ES configuration. All the ESI 
generated by AOS nodes will be based on Type 0x3 (Mac based) ESI as specified in the RFC 7432.
The Type 0x3 ESI allows for the most available space (9 octet) to specify the ESI value.
Following is the AOS model to construct a network unique 9-Byte ESI:
• For access ports configured on physical ports:
 
The 9 Octet is derived from the Port MAC of the access port:
–
0x3 + Access-Port-Mac+ 0xffffff
• For access ports configured on LACP:
The 9 Octet is derived from the CE MAC obtained from the LACP frames of the trunk port:
–
0x3 + CE-Mac+ 0xff + 0x<Key-Id>
• For access ports configured on static LinkAgg:
It is required to manually configure the network unique ESI for the static LinkAgg:
For the manual configuration of ESI, AOS EVPN will provide a 5-octet user input in the format 
specified below. The remaining 4-octet is reserved/internal to AOS to interpret the trunk information 
associated with the ESI.
The AOS manual ESI will use a 1-byte signature in the upper octet to ensure the global uniqueness of 
the configured ESI. 
The resulting format of the 9-octet ID is:
–
0x3 + 0xA1 + 5-byte-Manual-ESI-ID + 0xFF + 0x<Trunk-Id>

OmniSwitch ETag Model
The AOS ETag model provides an additional level of granularity in the management of FDB entries (L2 
and L3) of the EVPN based control plane by generation of ETag based routes. All SAP attachments 
configured on the EVPN enabled access ports will generate an ETag based route update. Route updates 
and withdrawals associated with the SAP attachments can be summarized at the ETag level rather than the 
withdrawal of routes associated with each MAC and host addresses associated with the ESI+ETag tuple.
The ETag value is the VLAN ID associated with the SAP.

EVPN Modes
• Singlehoming - Enables you to connect a customer edge (CE) device to one provider edge (PE) device. 
Singlehoming can be a physical port or a linkagg (connected to only one PE). The singlehoming mode 
of operation does not require Ethernet segment values to be configured. It is auto-generated. 
• Multihoming - Enables you to connect a customer edge (CE) device to more than one provider edge 
(PE) device. Multihoming ensures redundant connectivity. The redundant PE device ensures that there 
is no traffic disruption when there is a network failure. Following are the types of multihoming:
> Single-Active - Only a single PE, among all the PEs attached to an Ethernet segment, is allowed to 
forward traffic to that Ethernet segment for a given VLAN.
> All-Active - All the PEs attached to an Ethernet segment are allowed to forward known unicast traf-
fic to and from that Ethernet segment for a given VLAN.
Split Horizon 
Split horizon prevents the looping of broadcast, unknown unicast, and multicast (BUM) traffic in a 
network. The split horizon basic principle is simple: information about the routing for a particular packet 
is never sent back in the direction from which it was received.
Local Link Bias
Local Link Bias conserves bandwidth by using local links to forward unicast traffic exiting a Virtual 
Chassis or Virtual Chassis Fabric (VCF) that has a link aggregation group (LAG) bundle composed of 
member links on different member switches in the same Virtual Chassis or VCF. A local link is a member 
link in the LAG bundle that is on the member switch that received the traffic.
Aliasing
Remote nodes will use the route to load balance traffic forwarded to the peer PEs of the ES. This allows 
the remote PEs to establish a multi-path route to the multihoming ES.

VRF Based Tenancy Model for AOS EVPN Services
The EVPN service follow VRF based Tenancy model, which mandates the EVPN configurations to be 
executed under non-default VRF context including the show commands to view the EVPN specific 
configuration.
EVPN services can be provisioned as both L2 based and L3 based services.
For the services that are L2 based (when an IP/IRB interface is not associated with the service), the VRF 
will not be available to identify the operation boundary of the service. For the services that are L3 based, 
the service provisioning is detached from the creation of the IP interface, which is provisioned within the 
context of a VRF.
Bridge-Domains (BDs), which denote the access side VLAN ID of the customer network are attached to 
services. This is accomplished using the SAP configurations. Since, multiple customers can share common 
BDs, it is important to establish the BD to customer association so as to not mix or attach BDs to services 
that are provisioned in a different tenancy.
For example, 
vrf1 service 1, BD-10:service1
vrf1 service 2, BD-10:service2 
- this is not allowed since BD-10:vrf1 is already attached to service 1.
A generic operational boundary called the Tenancy is established within which the EVPN based services 
and the BD attachment to the services can operate in. While a tenancy can contain many services, a 
service can be associated with only one tenancy.
Multiple tenancies can be defined within the EVPN network based on geographic (for example, Floor1, 
Floor2, and so on), functional (DC-POD1, DC-Server, and son on), or Organizational (Engineering, 
Finance, Quality, and so on) needs of the network administrator.
For a typical Enterprise EVPN network, each VRF depicts a tenancy (one-to-one tenancy to VRF 
mapping). The configuration of the VRF as Tenancy for EVPN is explained with the following 
configuration example. In the given example, the access port configuration and provisioning of non-EVPN 
services are based on legacy model (VRF unaware model). EVPN based services and the attachment to 
these services (BD to service Mapping) are provisioned within the context of a VRF. 
The example depicts the service configuration including configuration of SPB service. There are two 
VRFs created (ct1 and ct2) that represents the two tenancies (customers) of this EVPN network. EVPN 
based services and the BD attachment to these services are created in both the VRFs.

-> service access port 1/1/6 vlan-xlation enable evpn-ethernet-segment enable
-> service access port 1/1/30 vlan-xlation enable evpn-ethernet-segment enable
-> service access linkagg 1 vlan-xlation enable evpn-ethernet-segment enable multi-
homing all-active esi 00:00:02:03:04
-> service access linkagg 10 vlan-xlation enable evpn-ethernet-segment enable 
multi-homing all-active esi 00:00:01:02:03
-> service access port 1/1/16 vlan-xlation enable
-> service 2000 spb isid 2000 bvlan 4000 vlan-xlation enable
-> service 2000 sap port 1/1/16:2000
VRF configuration
-> vrf create ct1

Configuring EVPN on Overlay Services
This section provides the information about how to configure and activate the OmniSwitch 
implementation of EVPN on overlay services:
• “Enabling/Disabling EVPN on a Service” on page 18-13.
• “Enabling/Disabling Ethernet Segment Operations on an Access Port” on page 18-15.
• “Configure a Service Access Point on an EVPN Service” on page 18-16
Note. Since EVPN service follow VRF based Tenancy model, BGP EVPN service must be enabled or 
disabled on a VXLAN service only in a non-default VRF context. And, EVPN service parameters (like 
the service and SAP provisioning, an IP/IRB interface, and so on) must be configured in the same VRF 
instance as the service. 
Enabling/Disabling EVPN on a Service
Use ‘BGP EVPN’ parameter in the service vxlan command to configure a Ethernet Virtual Private 
Network (EVPN) service. Currently, EVPN service can be configured only on a VXLAN service.
-> vrf create vrf1
vrf1::-> service 50 vxlan vnid 50 bgp-evpn enable
Use service bgp-evpn command to configure the EVPN service parameters.
For example:
-> vrf vrf1 service 50 igmp-mld-proxy enable
Further sections in the document describes the detailed steps to configure the service parameters under an 
EVPN service.
Enabling/Disabling Ethernet Segment Operations on an Access 
Port
Enable or disable Ethernet segment (ES) operations on an access port. To enable ES segment operations 
on an access port, use the evpn-ethernet-segment parameter in the service access command. When 
enabled, it allows EVPN ES configuration and functionality on a service access port. Single-homing is 
enabled on all physical access ports when ES is enabled on the port. Physical ports ES support only single 
homing.
- An access port/linkagg that is enabled for EVPN requires the port to be associated with EVPN Ethernet 
Segment Identifier (ESI). For physical and LACP access port, by default, a MAC based ESI is auto 
generated when EVPN ES is enabled based on the port MAC for physical port and based on CE 
(Customer Edge) MAC for trunk port. And for static linkagg access port, manually configure the ESI ID. 
Use the esi parameter to configure ESI. 
Use the multi-homing parameter to set the multihoming option to all-active or single-active.
> In all-active mode, all the PEs attached to the particular ES is allowed to forward traffic to and from 
that ES.

<<<PAGE 594>>>

Configuring EVPN on Overlay Services
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-16
> In single-active mode, only a single PE among a group of PEs attached to the particular ES is 
allowed to forward traffic to and from that ES.
> Multihoming mode (single-active or all-active) on ES cannot be modified at run-time. To modify 
multihoming option on an existing ES, disable or re-enable ES with new multihoming mode.
- Use the es_description parameter to add a description for the ES. When no description is provided, a 
default descriptor will be generated based on the access port ID.
For example, the following enables or disable ES operations on an access port using the service access 
command.
On a static lingkagg, ESI has to be provided for an ES.
-> service access linkagg 120 evpn-ethernet-segment enable esi 00:00:04:05:06
On a dynamic lingkagg, ESI is auto generated.
-> service access linkagg 121 evpn-ethernet-segment enable
On a physical port, ESI is auto generated.
-> service access port 1/1/3-10 evpn-ethernet-segment enable
To disable ES operation on an access port, use ‘disable’ option.
-> service access port 1/1/3-10 evpn-ethernet-segment disable
Configure a Service Access Point on an EVPN Service
Configure a Service Access Point (SAP) by associating a SAP ID with EVPN service. A SAP ID is 
comprised of a customer-facing port (referred to as an access port) and an encapsulation value that is used 
to identify the type of network traffic to map to the associated service (for example, service 10 sap port 1/
1/23:10, where 1/1/23:10 is the SAP ID).
When configuring a SAP for a EVPN service, the SAP and the SAP sub-configurations on an EVPN 
service must be executed in the context of a non-default VRF. This must be in the same VRF instance as 
the service VRF the SAP is being associated to.
For example:
Configuring a SAP on an EVPN service in non-default VRF instance same as the service instance:
-> vrf create vrf1
vrf1::-> service 50 vxlan vnid 50 bgp-evpn enable
vrf1::-> service 50 sap linkagg 120:10

EVPN Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB)
In the BGP EVPN network, the Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB) is defined in RFC 9135 to provide 
the inter-service routing. The IRB is a Layer 3 interface, which allows bridging and routing across 
different EVIs in an inter-subnet network. Each EVI is represented by a unique subnet. It uses the MAC-
VRF and IP-VRF to bridge and route the packets.
EVPN supports IRB functionality, which allows the PEs in a EVPN network to forward both Layer 2 
(bridged) and Layer 3 (routed) traffic. When a PE forwards Layer 2 traffic, it is said to be performing 
bridging. Similarly, when a PE forwards Layer 3 traffic, it is said to be performing routing. The traffic 
between different subnets is forwarded through the gateways.
The IRB supports two network models:
• Asymmetric IRB network
• Symmetric IRB network
The Asymmetric IRB performs routing only on the ingress PE, while Symmetric IRB performs routing on 
both ingress and egress PEs.
Asymmetric IRB
The Asymmetric IRB deployment is based on a stretched EVI design. It requires source and destination 
EVIs to be configured in both the PEs involved in the forwarding. Each EVI must be IRB enabled with an 
L3 interface on each PE.
The Asymmetric IRB operates in a Route plus Bridge forwarding on the ingress PE and a Bridge 
forwarding on the egress PE.
The Asymmetric IRB operation is explained using the below topology.
Figure 18-1: Asymmetric IRB Model

<<<PAGE 596>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
EVPN Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB)
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-18
Both the EVI1 and EVI2 are stretched across the PEs (PE1, PE2 and PE3). Additionally, the EVIs are IRB 
enabled on all the PEs where each PE assigns a unique L3 address for the subnet of that EVI.
Note. In this example PE (1,2) is used to indicate the peer nodes attached to dual homed host CE1. 
As such either PE1 or PE2 can participate in the routing of this frame based on CE1 load balancing 
towards the pair of PE (1,2):
• When the multi-homed CE1 10.10.10.15 hosted on PE1 and PE2 wants to forward to CE2 20.20.20.35, 
which is hosted by PE3, it requires the EVPN network to route the traffic between EVI1 and EVI2.
• CE1 will forward the frames to the Gateway PE (1,2) of 10.10.10.10 and the local router MAC of the 
PE (1,2).
• On PE (1,2), upon receiving the frame from CE1 destined to the local gateway, it will trigger a route 
lookup for destination IP 20.20.20.35. If the EVPN control frame has learned the host CE3, then the PE 
(1,2) would have received the RT-2 route notification from PE3 for this host CE3.
• PE (1,2) will now route the frame with destination IP CE3 towards the tunnel of PE3 and to EVI2. 
• Since the EVI2 is stretched between PE (1,2) and PE3, after routing the frame from EVI1 to EVI2 the 
frame will be bridged from PE1 to PE2 in EVI2 after the tunnel encapsulation.
• At PE3, the frame from PE (1,2) is tunnel terminated. Since frame is already bridged in EVI2, the 
destination MAC lookup will yield the attachment point of local host CE3. Frame will be bridged to 
CE3.
The Inter EVI packet forwarding (encapsulation and decapsulation) when using an Asymmetric IRB based 
EVPN network is shown in the diagram below:
Figure 18-2 : Inter EVI Packet Forwarding in Asymmetric IRB Based EVPN Network
PE1:
EVI1: 10.10.10.1/24
EVI2: 20.20.20.1/24
PE2:
EVI1: 10.10.10.2/24
EVI2: 20.20.20.2/24
PE3:
EVI1: 10.10.10.3/24
EVI2: 20.20.20.3/24

Configuring an Asymmetric IRB Interface
EVPN IRB (Integrated Routing and Bridging) feature enables a Layer 2 VPN and an Layer 3 VPN overlay 
that allows end hosts across the overlay to communicate with each other within the same subnet and 
across different subnets within the VPN.
For EVPN enabled service, specify the service parameter to configure an asymmetric IRB interface on a 
service. When an IP interface is configured on an EVPN enabled service, it is considered as an IRB 
interface. In case of asymmetric IRB, the services are stretched to all the access PEs (Provider Edge). 
When creating an IP interface for an EVPN enabled service, consider the following: The service ID 
specified must already exist in the switch configuration. Only IPv4 interface is supported.
To configure an IRB interface, use the ip interface command. For example:
-> vrf vrf1 ip interface evpn1 address 10.1.1.1/24 service 10
To configure an IRB interface with anycast gateway address, use the ip interface command with anycast-
gateway-address parameter. For example:
-> vrf vrf1 ip interface evpn1 address 10.1.1.1/24 service 10 anycast-gateway-
address 10.1.1.254

<<<PAGE 598>>>

Symmetric IRB
The operation of the Symmetric L3VPN model is simple in terms of configuration and deployment and 
also better scalability than the Asymmetric IRB mode, and therefore is the prevalent and recommended 
configuration for the inter-service routing of EVPN hosts. The symmetric IRB model is used for 
establishing L3 connectivity for both host-based and prefix-based routes.
In the symmetric IRB solution, a network unique EVI is created on all the PEs for each tenant/VRF of the 
PE. This EVI is configured as the L3EVI (referred as Fabric-vpn in AOS). Only one Fabric-vpn is 
required per VRF that will provide the inter-EVI reachability for all the IRB services in the VRF. 
Additionally, the Fabric-vpn is also used as the gateway for prefix route advertisement for both EVPN and 
non-EVPN routes.
Each customer/tenant of the VXLAN network is assigned a unique VRF. The VLAN-tag based traffic 
from the hosts are assigned to an IRB-EVI on the access side. A Fabric-vpn/L3EVI is provisioned in each 
tenancy for the inter-subnet routing among the subnets (IRB interfaces) and prefix routes of this tenant 
network. By default, all EVPN enabled services are designated with VPN type as ‘default’. So the service 
has to be explicitly configured as ‘Fabric-vpn’ VPN type to enable the perVRF symmetric IRB operation 
on that service EVI. 
All the IRB-EVI services within the VRF will be aware of the Fabric-vpn associated with the VRF. The 
forwarding path in the MAC-VRF entries use either bridge (using the L2EVI) or route (using the L3EVI) 
based forwarding. When a Fabric-vpn is configured for a VRF for symmetric IRB, the RT-2 MAC-VRF 
message to advertise the host entries are modified such that the remote hosts can either bridge or route to 
the host.
Figure 18-3 : Symmetric IRB Based EVPN Network

<<<PAGE 599>>>

OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide

page 18-21
Configuration and Operation of Symmetric IRB Interfaces
The configuration and operations of symmetric IRB router will have the following operations:
• The configuration and advertisement of the gateway interfaces of the Fabric-vpn. This includes setting 
up per VRF gateway reachability by configuring a Fabric-vpn type service, and associating it with 
per-VRF L3 interface.
• The service binding to a VRF will automatically allow BGP to receive all the local routes (host/prefix 
routes) and advertise them to the EVPN network. Host routes from local IRB services are advertised 
using BGP EVPN RT-2 type routes and prefix routes are advertised using BGP EVPN RT-5 routes.
• Only prefix route reachability of IRB interfaces is supported for single-homed attachments.
Configuring an L3VPN/Fabric Interface For Symmetric Routing
Configure a designated EVI service for symmetric IRB by configuring a EVPN service with type ‘fabric-
vpn’, creating a per-VRF L3 interface, and associating it with the Fabric-vpn service type.
To create a Fabric-vpn service type, use service vpn-type command. For example:
-> -> vrf vrf1 service 50 vpn-type fabric-vpn
Use ip interface command to create a per-VRF L3 interface, and associate it with the Fabric-vpn service 
type. For example:
-> vrf 1 ip interface vrf1-evpn-fabric-50 address 50.50.50.1/24 service 50
The IP association with the service will create an operationally enabled EVPN interface when the service 
is of type Fabric-vpn and the service is BGP EVPN enabled. Only one fabric interface is allowed per VRF. 
Prefix Route Distribution Using the IRB Fabric-vpn Service 
This section details the handling of prefix-based routes in an EVPN network as detailed in RFC 9136. 
The RT5 route is implemented in BGP EVPN to address the reachability for prefix routes that are sourced 
from non-EVPN interface attachments and EVPN access connections (single-homed and multi-homed).
There are multiple models and deployment topologies that can be implemented to support the basic 
reachability requirements for prefix-based routes from the host devices connected to an EVPN network. 
The following two models are supported for reachability of prefix-based routes.
• External network reachability through a Border Leaf Node.
• Prefix routes reachable through IRB interfaces.

<<<PAGE 600>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
EVPN Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB)
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-22
External Network Reachability Through a Border Leaf Node
The basic requirement for prefix-based routing is to provide access to external network for the host 
devices of an EVPN network. This model is supported with symmetric based routing, hence, it is 
mandatory to configure a Fabric-vpn service for the PE(s) that need reachability to the prefix route. 
Typically, one PE node in the EVPN network will act as a border leaf to the external network. This PE 
will act as the gateway node for all other PEs of the EVPN network for their hosts to route to external 
networks.
The route advertisement procedures and reachability for the network is detailed with the example given 
below.
Figure 18-4 : External Network Reachability Through a Border Leaf Node
• In the example above, the border Leaf-1 has reachability to external route 192.168.0.X/24 in VRF-2. 
The EVPN network hosts ESI-1, ESI-123 and ESI-4 that are spread across different PE nodes of the 
network and are operational in VRF-1. 
• For the hosts attached to the ESIs to be able to reach the external network, a Fabric-EVI interface 
(EVI-50) and a gateway interface IP (50.50.50.PEx) must be configured across all the PEs, which host 
these ESIs. The Border Leaf-1 exports the routes from the VRF-2 to the GRM (Global Route 
Manager). 
• The Fabric-EVI interface (EVI-50) on the border-leaf node registers with the GRM to receive the 
routes from this VRF (VRF-2). The GRM then redistribute the routes from VRF-2 to EVI-50.
• The Border Leaf PE1 now advertises the RT5 based routes for this prefix route as: RDPE1-LB0:VRF-
1, Prefix Address -192.168.0.0, Prefix Length - 24, ESI - 0, ETag - 0, GW IP - 50.50.50.1, Label - 50.
• The remote PEs will import the RT5 into the inRIB if there is a matching RT configured on that PE 
(for example, for EVI-50).

<<<PAGE 601>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
EVPN Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB)
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-23
• The route will be parsed and forwarded to the GRM with gateway information of Fabric:PE-gateway 
IP (EVI-50: 50.50.50.1).
• The VRF-1 on the remote PEs will import the routes from GRM and inserts the route in the RIB. Any 
hosts on this VRF can now establish reachability to the external route.
The given example highlights the reachability for the host, any other VRF can import this route and 
establish local connectivity to the external network. In the case of reachability for local hosts on the border 
Leaf (PE1:ESI-1), the route must be redistributed between the VRFs (in this case, from VRF2 to VRF1).
Prefix Routes Reachable Through IRB Interfaces
When routing-enabled CE devices are connected to the access port (either physical port or trunk port) of 
the EVPN network, the route management mechanism can be enhanced to take advantage of the EVPN 
based operations available for the access attachments prefix routes that are reachable behind a CE node 
can be advertised with ESI and E-tag information to allow for mass updates and multi-homing operations. 
Prefix routes can thus make use of the multi-path redundancy and quick convergence for access 
attachments to an EVPN network. This is a deviation from how traditional route advertisement is based on 
a gateway IP interface(s).
Currently, prefix route reachability for single-homed attachments is supported when Fabric-vpn service is 
available for the IRB interface of the attached node.
Figure 18-5 : Prefix Routes Reachable Through IRB Interfaces

• In the example above, border Leaf-1 has IRB interface (Intf 10) enabled in VRF-1 for routing with 
single homed CE device (CE1). Additionally, a Fabric-EVI interface (EVI-50:IP-50.50.50.PEx) is 
created in the same VRF across all the PE nodes of the EVPN network.
• The CE attachment identified by ESI-1 has established a routing protocol adjacency (example, OSPF) 
with Intf-10 of PE1. 
• The gateway for this CE (10.10.10.20) is advertising reachability to external route 192.168.0.X/24 and 
192.168.1.X/24.
• ESI-123 and ESI-4 that are spread across different PE nodes of the network and are operational in 
VRF-1. The above routes are added to the VRF-1 route database with gateway pointing to 
CE1:Intf10:GW-10.10.10.20.
• The VRF-1 instance on the border leaf1 exports the routes to the GRM. 
• The Fabric-EVI interface (EVI-50) on this node registers with the GRM to receive the routes from this 
VRF (auto-bind when Fabric-EVI is L3 enabled).
• The GRM then redistributes the routes from VRF-1 to EVI-50. 
• BGP EVPN will receive the routes with the route GW information. PE1 can now advertise RT5 based 
routes for this prefix route. If a Fabric-EVI interface is already configured for the VRF, then the route 
is resolved to be reachable from other PEs through the routed Fabric-EVI interface. The RT5 is 
constructed with the Fabric-EVI label and gateway IP.
Route Redistribution for Prefix Route Advertisement for 
Symmetric IRB
When a Fabric-vpn service is created on a particular VRF, it triggers BGP EVPN to auto import all routes 
exported by fabric-service VRF. A redistribution configuration is required to support importing of routes 
so that BGP EVPN can register for route imports from additional VRFs. 
Use service redist source-vrf command to configure route redistribution. 
For example,
-> vrf vrf1 service 50 redist source-vrf VRF-2 all-routes
With this configuration, the EVI associated with the Fabric-vpn type service will register with GRM to 
import all the routes from the specified source VRF (for example, VRF2). This is in addition to the EVI 
registered for its home VRF (for example, considering VRF1 as the home VRF).
The ‘redist source-vrf’ is configurable only for services with type ‘fabric-vpn’. 
When routes are redistributed across VRFs, the inter-VRF export and import of the route has to be 
configured in the home-VRF of the fabric EVI and also the source VRF such that there is reachability 
established through both the VRFs in the data plane of the IP module.
See “Route-Redistribution for Fabric-EVI Services Configuration Example” on page 18-54

Route Redistribution (VLAN-Based Hand-off) on the Border 
Nodes
Border-Nodes provide external connectivity to the EVPN network. Typically, a pair of redundant nodes 
with similar node designation (Border-Leaf or Border-Spine) are provisioned to provide multi-path 
connectivity between the external network and the EVPN network of the local site or PoD (Point of 
Delivery) as shown in the below network diagram.
Figure 18-6 : Route Redistribution (VLAN-Based Hand-off) on the Border Nodes
It is expected that the network admin will follow the below described standard route policies when 
managing the route distribution between the External Network and the Local EVPN network.
This example uses OSPF as the routing protocol for route advertisement between the EVPN and external 
network.
Scenario 1 - Managing the local host-routes advertisement from the border-node to external 
network
The Border-leaf will import all the site local routes (host and prefix routes) from the PE nodes. Generally, 
the site-local routes are reachable from the border-leaf through the perVRF Fabric-vpn. These routes will 
be redistributed to the OSPF routing interface to advertise them to the external network.
When there is a large number of host routes that are advertised through the EVPN BGP RT2 messages, the 
border leaf will advertise all the host routes to the external network leading to excessive load in both the 
control-plane and the data-plane of the external router. In this case, there is a need to summarize the host 
routes under the subnet of their IRB interface.
A route-map policy needs to be defined with a specific access-list. This access-list will contain only the 
aggregate route for each IRB subnets of the EVPN network. The route redistribution from EVPN to OSPF 
must include only the routes that match this route-map policy. All other routes such as the host-routes will 
be omitted from the redistribution.

<<<PAGE 604>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
EVPN Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB)
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-26
An example configuration of the route summarization or aggregation on the border-node:
-> vrf vrf1 ip access-list "IRB-SUBNETS"
-> vrf vrf1 ip access-list "IRB-SUBNETS" address 30.0.0.0/8 action permit 
redist-control aggregate
-> vrf vrf1 ip access-list "IRB-SUBNETS" address 40.40.0.0/16 action permit 
redist-control aggregate
-> vrf vrf1 ip route-map "IRB-SUBNETS" sequence-number 8 action permit
-> vrf vrf1 ip route-map "IRB-SUBNETS" sequence-number 8 match ip-address "IRB-
SUBNETS"
-> vrf vrf1 ip redist import into ospf route-map "IRB-SUBNETS" admin-state 
enable
In the above example, an access-list is created to contain the summarized hosts from two IRB interfaces 
(30.0.0.0/8 and 40.40.0.0/16) of the local EVPN network. When the border-node redistributes the local 
import routes to OSPF, a route-map is applied using the above access-list in order to only advertise the 
aggregated host route information.
Scenario 2- When the two Border-Nodes are connected to external router(s), it is possible for the 
external router to echo a route from one border-node back to the other border-node.
The attached remote hosts and the IRB prefix route associated with the hosts of the EVPN network is 
advertised to the EVPN network using Route Type RT2 and RT5 respectively. The border-node will 
register with the GRM (Global Route Manager) to import these host and IRB prefix routes into its data-
plane. These prefix routes will then be advertised to the external router using the OSPF interface.
In the external router, the routes received from OSPF session to one border-node can be forwarded back to 
the other border leak OSPF session causing the IRB prefix route to be echoed back from one border-node 
to the other border-node.
On the border-node, these routes received from the external on the OSPF interface will cause a multi-path 
reachability for the host (one being through the route imported from the BGP control plane and other 
being the echo of the route from the External router). 
To prevent this behavior, the import routes must be configured to have a higher route-preference (lower 
value than OSPF) than the OSPF routes. This will ensure that the host has only one direct tunnel path from 
the border-node to a local PE. The default setting is for import routes have a lower precedence than OSPF.
For example:
-> vrf vrf1 ip route-pref import 100
Currently, only OSPF routing protocol is supported for external connectivity with border leaf. And, the 
above route-preference configuration is required. In both the scenarios, the recommended setting is to be 
configured in all the tenancy VRFs where the fabric service and IRB services are provisioned on the 
border-node.

Distributed Anycast Gateway (DAG) for EVPN 
In a large network, for example, Data center network, there will be host mobility among the PE nodes of 
the connected service. To support large scalable networks, such mobility must be managed with 
efficiency. DAG supports this host mobility without the need for any added redundancy protocols for the 
EVI service.
A distributed Anycast address called the Anycast IP Address is configured on all the PEs that share the 
EVI. Along with the anycast IP, an anycast MAC-address (virtual MAC) is configured on all the common 
PEs. This anycast MAC is set up per VRF and the same anycast MAC address is used for all subnet 
anycast IP interfaces of the VRFs.
Figure 18-7 : Host Mobility with Support for Default Gateway (Anycast-IP and Anycast-MAC) for the 
IRB enabled EVI
As shown in the example, the VM1 is configured with the default anycast gateway 10.10.10.10 along with 
the configured VMAC 00:20:DA:01:01:01. In case of the VM1 mobility from CE1 to CE2, the gateway 
and its MAC will remain the same and the host does not need to re-ARP for an updated gateway. This 
allows seamless L2 mobility for the host among the PEs without the need to update the default gateway of 
the host.
In the above given EVPN network, the host addresses (VM1 and VM2) are advertised by EVPN using the 
Route Type-2 updates, which contain the MAC+IP of the host. An update is generated for each of the host 
discovered by an attached PE. The MAC-VRF for EVI-10 and EVI-20 will be updated with the host 
address entries on all the participation PEs that have the matching EVI as advertised in the Route Type-2 
update.

<<<PAGE 606>>>

Anycast Gateway Configuration to Support Multi-homed 
Ethernet-Segments
Anycast Gateway configuration is critical while deploying multi-homed Ethernet Segments (MH-ES) of 
the EVPN network. 
The ability to seamlessly forward traffic from the CE to any of its connected gateway nodes requires that 
the CE be aware of a common gateway interface that is shared among all the Peer Nodes of the MH-ES.
Anycast gateway configuration will provide uninterrupted network access from the CE even when there is 
loss of connectivity to any of its multi-homed PEs. Therefore, it is essential to provide support for anycast 
gateway for IRB services that are attached to multi-homed attachments.
This following example demonstrates the need for anycast gateways for IRB enabled EVIs when 
connecting to multi-homed hosts.
Figure 18-8 : Anycast Gateway Support for Multihomed Clients of an EVPN Network
Here, the edge device CE1 is multi-homed to PE1 and PE2 through a multi-homed trunk link. The CE1 
bridge domain VLAN 10 is attached to IRB interface of EVI1. This IRB interface is configured with the 
anycast gateway in addition to the primary IP. The CE1 is configured with the default gateway of this 
anycast address 10.10.10.10. 
Both PE1 and PE2 will advertise the anycast gateway 10.10.10.10 (and the auto generated anycast MAC 
00:5E:00:00:01:01) as the SIP of this IRB EVI1 when forwarding control frames towards the access 
attachments. The primary IP of the IRB EVI is never visible to the access attachments.
There is a similarly multi-homed IRB configuration on the nodes PE3 and PE4, which is hosting CE2 in 
the bridge domain vlan 20. When CE1 host 10.10.10.15 wants to route to remote CE2 20.20.20.15 in 
subnet 20, it will forward the frames to the anycast gateway 10.10.10.10 (hosted by PE (1,2)). The frame 
can take either of the trunk links of this multi-homed host.

<<<PAGE 607>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
Distributed Anycast Gateway (DAG) for EVPN
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-29
For the frame received on PE (1,2), since it is destined to the local anycast router (DA-MAC = Anycast 
Mac 00:5E:00:00:01:01), this will trigger a route lookup for DIP 20.20.20.15. The frame will be routed by 
PE (1,2) towards PE3.
When routing into the EVPN network, the forwarding PE will use its local router interface as the source 
address (for example, PE1 RTR MAC) and not the anycast MAC. Similarly, the destination address of the 
routed frame will be the router MAC of PE3. Thus, the network routing uses the router MAC while 
routing on the edge (access) will use the anycast MAC.
PE3 will then route/bridge the frame to CE2.
Note: It is required to manually configure the anycast interface as the default gateway on the CE nodes.
Configuring Distributed Anycast Gateway for EVPN
Use the ip anycast-gateway-mac command to configure anycast MAC address. Anycast MAC can be 
auto derived or configured manually. 
Use the mac_address parameter to configure the anycast MAC address manually. This MAC is utilized 
by all DAG enabled VPN services to enable route lookup on access ports. All the PEs for a given tenant 
subnet use the same anycast default gateway IP and MAC addresses.
Auto-derivation of the anycast MAC can only be used if there is a certainty that the auto-derived MAC 
does not collide with any MAC address that is already being used in the network. An anycast MAC-
address is configured on all the common VTEPs, This anycast MAC address must be configured per VRF 
and the same anycast MAC address is used for all subnet anycast IP interfaces of a VRF.
For example:
-> vrf vrf1 ip anycast-gateway-mac auto
-> vrf vrf1 ip anycast-gateway-mac 00:00:05:01:01:04
Use the no option to remove the configuration.
-> vrf vrf1 no ip anycast-gateway-mac
To attach an anycast gateway address to an IRB interface, use ip interface anycast-gateway-address 
command. This is to avoid configuring the gateway on the CEs (Customer Edge) when the host moves 
across the access PEs on the EVPN network.
Anycast gateway MAC address needs to be configured first before configuring anycast gateway address, 
and anycast gateway address must be configured after the primary address is configured on the service.
For example:
-> vrf vrf1 ip interface ips100 address 10.1.1.1/24 service 10
-> vrf vrf1 ip interface ips100 anycast-gateway-address 50.50.50.254
Use the no option to remove the configuration.
-> vrf vrf1 no ip interface ips100 anycast-gateway-address 50.50.50.254

<<<PAGE 608>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
IP Multicast Services for EVPN
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide

page 18-30
IP Multicast Services for EVPN
IGMP and MLD (V4 and V6) snooping and proxying functionality can be enabled or disabled for a EVPN 
enabled service. Supports enabling or disabling SMET (Selective Multicast Ethernet Tag) capability, and 
setting the SMET on multihome capability with Designated Forwarder options.
SMET capability
By default, SMET capability is disabled. In this mode, the PE (Provider Edge) runs in IMET (Inclusive 
Multicast Ethernet Tag) mode, wherein all the other PEs will forward every multicast stream to this PE. 
If IGMP or MLD proxy is enabled, with SMET capability disable, then, only the traffic from network-to-
access and access-to-access will be forwarded. When SMET capability is enabled, the PE runs in SMET 
mode, wherein the remote PEs will forward the multicast traffic only for the groups that this PE requests. 
SMET capability can be enabled only when IGMP or MLD proxy is enabled. 
SMET on multihome capability
SMET on multihome option can be set to either ‘DF’ or ‘all’.
By default, SMET on multihome option is set to ‘DF’. When set to this option, only the designed PE (DF) 
will originate SMET routes (RT6) for the groups learned on the multihomed ES. The multicast traffic 
from remote PEs will be sent to the DF PE, and then gets forwarded over the respective SAPs. In the event 
of the DF change, some traffic drop to clients can be seen, as the remote PEs will continue to forward the 
traffic to older PE until they receive the SMET routes form the new PE. This can be addressed by setting 
the SMET on multihome option to ‘all’.
When SMET on multihome is set to ‘all’ option, it helps in minimizing the traffic loss in DF change 
events. By enabling this option, all the PEs will originate SMET (RT6) routes. So, the remote PEs receive 
SMETs form all the PEs of the multihomed ES and forwards the traffic to all the PEs. But, the traffic will 
be forwarded only by the DF to the SAPs. In case of a DF change event, the new elected DF will start 
forwarding the traffic as it is already receiving traffic from the remote PEs. This way the traffic loss is 
minimized.

<<<PAGE 609>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
IP Multicast Services for EVPN
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-31
Enabling/Disabling IP Multicast Services for EVPN
IGMP and MLD (V4 and V6) multicast snooping and proxying functionality can be enabled or disabled 
on a EVPN service using service igmp-mld-proxy command. 
Currently, MLD proxy is not supported.
When enabled, IGMP multicast snooping and proxying functionality is enabled on a service. When 
disabled, multicast traffic is flooded to all IMET/SMET nodes and is considered as unknown multicast.
For example:
The following enables both IGMP and MLD proxy along with SMET on the EVPN service.
-> vrf vrf1 service 100 igmp-mld-proxy enable smet-capability enable smet-on-
multihome df
The following enables only IGMP proxy along with SMET on the EVPN service. 
To enable only IGMP or only MLD proxy, the other one has to be disabled. That is, to enable IGMP 
proxy, disable MLD proxy (service service_id mld-proxy disable) and to enable only MLD proxy, disable 
IGMP proxy (service service_id igmp-proxy disable).
-> vrf vrf1 service 100 igmp-mld-proxy enable mld-proxy disable smet-capability 
enable smet-on-multihome df
IP Multicast Switching and Routing on the EVPN service cannot be configured using the IP multicast 
command ('ip multicast <service-id> admin-state").
However, when IGMP and MLD proxy is enabled on the EVPN service, the following multicast 
attributes/parameters are enabled default, with their default values. If necessary, use the specified 
commands to change the default values.
- ip multicast service <service_id> query-interval <time>
- ip multicast service <service_id> query-response-interval <time>
- ip multicast service <service_id> last-member-query-interval <time>
- ip multicast service <service_id> robustness <num>
- ip multicast service <service_id> source-timeout <time>
Note. On OmniSwitch 6870, deploying EVPN with IGMP proxy functionality requires enabling IGMP 
proxy across the EVPN domain.

<<<PAGE 610>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
Optimized Inter-Subnet Multicast Routing
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-32
Optimized Inter-Subnet Multicast Routing
OISM (Optimized Inter-subnet Multicast) is an EVPN-based solution that optimizes how IP multicast 
traffic is forwarded across different subnets within a network. OISM is standardized in RFC9625. It 
specifies a solution for multicast routing across different IP subnets of a tenant using fabric IRB routing 
interface. This does not require any native multicast routing protocols, like PIM (Protocol Independent 
Multicast). In RFC 9625, fabric IRB is referred as SBD (Supplemental Bridge Domain) and the user 
services as BD (Bridge Domain). Multicast routing across different tenants (VRF) is not in the scope of 
OISM.
Consider a scenario where a tenant (VRF) network is spread across four sites connected across EVPN 
core. Each of the sites are in a specific IP subnet (each mapped to a different service). Fabric IRB service 
is configured on all four PEs that are connecting these sites. Using this fabric IRB service, a multicast 
sources/clients from a given site will be able to send and receive multicast traffic from the other sites. 
Figure 18-9 : Optimized Inter-Subnet Multicast Routing Scenario
Let us consider a scenario where multicast client in Site1 is interested in receiving traffic from a multicast 
source in Site4. Site-1 is connected to PE1 through CE1. Fabric service (100) is configured on all four PEs 
and OISM is enabled. Service 10 is configured on PE1 to connect site-1 subnet to the network. Also, 
service 40 configured on PE-4 to connect site-4 to the network.
When PE1 receives IGMP join from CE1, PE1 generates an Selective Multicast Ethernet Tag (SMET) 
route for the multicast group to all the remote PEs. As OISM routing is enabled, SMET route is advertised 
with EVI of the fabric service. PE4 imports this route and creates a multicast group entry in fabric service.
When PE4 receives the first packet from site-4 multicast source, it creates route forward entry from 
service 40 to service 100. Once PE1 receives the first multicast traffic on fabric service 100, it forwards 
the traffic to client in site-1.
Use the multicast group show commands (show ip multicast group all-VRF, show ip multicast forward all-
VRF) to view the multicast group membership and forward entries for the OISM enabled service.

<<<PAGE 611>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
Optimized Inter-Subnet Multicast Routing
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-33
Enabling/Disabling OISM on a Fabric-IRB Service
Enable or disable OISM on an EVPN service by using the service oism command. By default, OISM is 
disabled on the fabric service. OISM can be configured on a fabric-VPN service only.
For example:
-> vrf vrf1 service 10 oism enable
-> vrf vrf1 service 10 oism disable

<<<PAGE 612>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
PIM-EVPN Gateway
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-34
PIM-EVPN Gateway
The interworking between the EVPN fabric and an external PIM router is called PIM EVPN Gateway 
(PEG). A PIM-EVPN Gateway (PEG) acts as the bridge between an EVPN network and an external 
Protocol-Independent Multicast (PIM) domain, while OISM (Optimized Inter-Subnet Multicast) is a 
feature that optimizes multicast traffic routing within the EVPN fabric by selectively forwarding traffic 
only to interested receivers. The PEG feature enables the border leaf nodes in the EVPN network to 
interwork with external PIM enabled networks so that multicast receivers or senders in the EVPN will be 
able to receive or send multicast traffic from or to the senders/receivers in external PIM network, while 
OISM improves efficiency for traffic between subnets inside the fabric.
The below diagram shows a network with multicast receivers or senders spread across EVPN and PIM 
networks. 
Figure 18-10 : PIM-EVPN Gateway Interworking Scenario
In the given scenario, PE1 and PE2 are leaf nodes hosting user services. PEG1 and PEG2 are border leaf 
nodes which are acting as PIM-EVPN gateways connecting EVPN network and the external PIM network. 
RP should always be hosted in external PIM router. PEG nodes cannot act as RP. Multicast receivers and 
sources are spread across EVPN and PIM networks. Multicast receivers inside EVPN are referred as 
internal receivers and the receivers in external PIM domain are referred as external receivers. Similarly, 
sources in EVPN are referred as internal sources and sources in PIM domain are referred as external 
sources. 
PEG1 and PEG2 acts a redundant pair for a given VRF and supports load balancing across different VRFs. 
One of the PEGs will be elected as a a DR (Designated Router) and that PEG node is responsible to 
interwork with external PIM network.
A PIM interface must be configured on the fabric service on both PEG1 and PEG2, and another PIM 
interface over VLAN towards the external PIM network. 
Currently, multicast receivers or sources connected directly to border nodes (PEGs) are not supported.

<<<PAGE 613>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
PIM-EVPN Gateway
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-35
External source to internal receivers
Consider R1 as an internal receiver requesting multicast traffic sent by the external source S5 connected to 
RP. When CE2 receives IGMP report from R1, it sends out RT6 route. Both PEGs receive this RT6 route, 
but PEG1 being the DR on the fabric PIM interface initiates PIM join towards the RP. When RP receives 
the traffic from S5, it forwards the traffic to PEG1, which further forwards it towards the receiver R1. 
Internal source to external receivers
To discover internal sources in EVPN, RFC proposes the concept default SBD-SMET route(*,*). Both 
PEGs send this default route to notify all other PEs in the fabric service. Thus, leaf PEs will forward every 
multicast flow to PEGs. This way PEGs discover all the multicast sources in the EVPN network, but only 
PEG DR registers all those sources to the RP.
Consider R5 as an external receiver connected to RP requesting multicast traffic sent by the internal 
source S2 connected to CE2. Both PEG1 and PEG2 generates default SBD-SMET route on the fabric to 
notify the leaf PEs. When PE2 receives multicast traffic from S2, it forwards all the traffic to both PEG1 
and PEG2 as they generated default route. PEG1 being the DR, it triggers PIM source registration with the 
RP. Once RP knows about this source, it sends (S,G) join towards either PEG1 or PEG2 depending upon 
the best unicast path to source S2. Whichever PEG receives the (S,G) from RP will forward the traffic to 
RP.
Alternate reachability to RP
PEG DR should always have reachability to RP for PIM-EVPN interworking to avoid traffic outage. If 
PEGs have only one link to the external PIM network, it might lead to single point of failure. To mitigate 
such scenarios, a backup PIM interface over a VLAN can be configured between PEGs, which provides an 
alternate path to RP when the primary link is down.
PEG DR election
PEG DR election can be done two methods:
• Native PIM hello based DR election
By configuring PIM interfaces on fabric interfaces of PEGs, PIM DR election logic selects one of the 
PEGs as DR for the fabric PIM interface. Elected PEG DR will perform the EVPN-PIM interworking 
procedures. This is the recommended DR election method.
• DR election based on DF election algorithm
PEG DR is elected based on DF election algorithm (similar to DF election in multi-homed Ethernet 
Segment based on RFC 9625). To use this method, PIM gateway configuration must be enabled on the 
fabric service. Also, PIM interfaces on the fabric service must be configured as stub interface to disable 
the native PIM DR election. 
Enable PIM DR Election Based on DF Election Algorithm
To enable or disable PIM DR (Designated Router) election based on DF election algorithm (similar to DF 
election in multi-homed Ethernet Segment) on the fabric service, use service pim-gateway command. By 
default, this is disabled. It is mandatory to enable OISM on the fabric service to enable this functionality.
For example:
-> vrf vrf1 service 10 pim-gateway enable
-> vrf vrf1 service 10 pim-gateway disable

<<<PAGE 614>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
MAC Mobility Service for EVPN
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-36
MAC Mobility Service for EVPN
MAC mobility is a scenario where a host moves from one Ethernet segment to another segment in the 
EVPN network.
If a CE MAC address is constantly moving between two different Ethernet segments, it will cause the 
address to be learned on a different PE each time. This is called MAC duplications and can be a result of a 
loop in the ES network or if the same address is present in two hosts of the service. Such a behavior leads 
to a continuous exchange of the MAC being advertised and withdrawn in the control plane among all the 
PEs in the EVPN network and leads to degradation of the EVPN network performance. This can be 
avoided by enabling MAC mobility feature for the EVPN enabled service. 
When MAC mobility loop protection is enabled, and if a PE detects a MAC mobility event through local 
learning, it starts the timeout value. In case, it detects that MAC moves count has reached the threshold 
count before the timer expires, it concludes that a duplicate MAC situation has occurred. The PE then 
alerts to stop sending, updating, or processing any BGP MAC advertisement routes for that MAC address 
until a corrective action is taken, and that MAC address is considered for hold-down. After completion of 
the retry-time interval, the MAC is moved out of hold-down and is flushed to restart the process of 
duplicate detection.
Configuring MAC Mobility Parameters for EVPN
To enable or disable MAC mobility loop protection for an EVPN service, use service bgp-evpn mac-
mobility command. By default, loop-protection is enabled. MAC mobility parameters like retry-time, 
threshold count, and timeout value can be configured using this command. 
For example:
-> service bgp-evpn mac-mobility loop-protection enable threshold 10 timeout 500 
retry-time 500

<<<PAGE 615>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
IP Mobility Service for EVPN
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-37
IP Mobility Service for EVPN
DAD (Duplicate Address Detection) is considered as movement of IP to MAC association. This means 
two hosts are assigned to the same IP. This could be either because of human error or a spoofing attack on 
an EVPN network. 
Duplicate IP detection monitors N "IP-moves" within M-second timer. If there are N moves within M time 
interval, then the host is moved to "filtering state" (F state) for a hold-down time of (3 *M - default).
Consider a scenario, where the ARP was learned on PE1 from host1 (macA). Now, a new ARP with the 
same IP from Host2 (macB) entering to the EVPN network is considered as IP Mobility. When an existing 
host is modified with a different MAC, a PE starts a M-second timer (duplicate detection interval), and if 
it detects N IP moves (threshold count) before the timer expires, it concludes that a duplicate IP situation 
has occurred. 
To detect the duplicate IP faster, the PE will send a Confirm message to the former owner of the IP. A 
Confirm message is a unicast ARP request message sent by the PE to the MAC addresses that previously 
owned the IP. If the PE does not receive an answer within a given time (CE confirm timeout), the new 
host will be confirmed and activated. If there are N moves within M-second time interval, then the host is 
moved to "filtering state" (F state) for a hold-down time interval. After the hold-down timer expires, the 
host that was in filtering state will be removed.
While a PE sends CONFIRM message to CE to probe for its local presence, the PE shall activate the 
remote host (during this confirm time). This is because the route is owned and activated by the new PE 
and other PEs in the network have updated the host route to this new PE. The new PE route has a higher 
sequence number and thats the reason its activated.
Configuring IP Mobility Parameters for EVPN
IP mobility parameters like duplicate IP detection interval, IP move threshold count, hold-down timer, and 
ce-confirm timeout can be modified using service bgp-evpn ip-mobility command. 
For example:
-> service bgp-evpn ip-mobility duplicate-ip-detection-interval 200 
ip-move-threshold 10

Configuring Service Proxy ARP Parameters for 
EVPN
Enabling the proxy ARP will check for the local proxy-ARP cache and generates an ARP reply if target IP 
is found, otherwise those ARP requests will be flooded in the targeted EVPN service. By default, Proxy 
ARP is enabled for an EVPN enabled service.
Configure the proxy ARP attributes for an EVPN service using the service proxy-arp command.
Service proxy parameters like ARP probe (enabled by default), ARP suppression (default value - 
complete), and ARP unknown options (default - discard) can be configured using the service proxy 
command. Currently, Proxy ARP command is supported only with the default values. Modification of 
these attributes are not supported.
For example:
-> vrf vrf1 service 100 proxy-arp arp-probe enable
-> vrf vrf1 service 100 proxy-arp arp-probe enable arp-suppression complete

EVPN Service Interface Models
RFC 8388 defines three types of EVPN service interface models for provisioning CE-VID to EVI.
• VLAN-based service interface model - In this model, each VLAN is mapped to one bridge domain and 
one EVI. There is a strict one-to-one mapping of VLAN to EVI, resulting in a separate bridge table for 
each VLAN.
Figure 18-11 : VLAN-based Service Interface Medel
• VLAN-bundle service interface model- In this model, multiple VLANs share the same bridge-domain 
and is mapped to one EVI, thus reducing the number of routes and labels stored in the table.
Figure 18-12 : VLAN-bundle Service Interface Model
• VLAN-aware bundle service interface - In this model, each VLAN is associated to one bridge domain 
but multiple such domains can be mapped to one EVI.

<<<PAGE 618>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
EVPN Service Interface Models
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-40
Figure 18-13 : VLAN-aware Bundle Service Interface
ALE Defined Service Based Interface Model (Enhanced VLAN- 
Bundle Service Interface)
AOS supports ALE defined service-based interface model, called, Enhanced VLAN-bundle service 
interface. This model is similar to VLAN-aware-bundle where ETags are carried in the RT1 (EAD per 
EVI) and RT2. However, VLAN-aware bundle mandates RT3 per ETag for the same EVI to achieve 
different broadcast domain. In case of ALE model, only one RT3 is generated for an EVI, which is 
applicable to all ETAG (hence ETAG =0). This reduces the number of RT3 routes in the network. The 
data plane mimics VLAN-bundle service interface model. This means that MAC addresses across 
different ETags belonging to same EVI will not be allowed and considered as move. 
Figure 18-14 : ALE Defined Service-based Interface Model - Enhanced VLAN-bundle Service Interface

The above hierarchy translates to following routes:
Why ALE Model?
• With awareness of tag in RT1 (EAD per EVI) and RT2, when a SAP is disabled or deleted, hierarchy 
is followed. All the FDB (RT2) on the SAP can be flushed without generating individual route 
withdraws.
• Withdraw of macro-objects triggering implicit delete of micro-objects reduces load in control plane 
exchange.
• ALE model is almost like VLAN-aware-bundle where ETags are carried in the RT1 (EAD per EVI) 
and RT2. However, VLAN-aware mandates RT3 per ETag for the same EVI to achieve different 
broadcast domain. In case of ALE model, only one RT3 is generated for EVI, which is applicable to all 
ETags (hence etag=0). This reduces the number of RT3 routes in the network. The data plane mimics 
VLAN-bundle service interface model. This means that mac across different ETags belonging to same 
EVI will not be allowed and considered as move. 
• In this model, VLAN-translation is enabled on the egress PE.

Configuring Service Interface Model
Use service bgp-evpn bridge-type command to configure the service interface model on a service. 
Select the bridge-type option as vlan-based to configure the VLAN-based service interface model, which 
has a one-to-one mapping of VLAN to bridge to service (EVI). 
Select the bridge-type option as enhanced-vlan-bundle to configure the Enhanced VLAN-bundle service 
interface model, which is unique to ALE for optimal performance in control plane. 
For example:
-> vrf vrf1 service 10 bgp-evpn enable bridge-type vlan-based
-> vrf vrf1 service 10 bgp-evpn enable bridge-type enhanced-vlan-bundle
EVPN Service BUM Traffic Management
BUM traffic (Broadcast, Unknown-Unicast and Multicast) traffic can each be managed for the flood or no 
flood treatment. Any action on each of these traffic type can be configured by enabling or disabling the 
flood action. By default, unknown multicast traffic will be flooded. Broadcast and unknown-unicast will 
have no flood action.
Currently, only the broadcast option can be changed to enable mode (from default state of disable). 
Unknown-unicast will only support disable and unknown-multicast will only support the enable mode.
To enable or disable flood action on the broadcast traffic, use service bgp-evpn broadcast command. By 
default, AOS blocks all broadcast and unknown unicast traffic from flooding to the network tunnels. Only 
unknown multicast can be flooded to the EVPN network tunnels of a service.
For example:
-> vrf vrf1 service 50 bgp-evpn broadcast enable
-> vrf vrf1 service 50 bgp-evpn broadcast disable

BGP Route Reflector for EVPN Routes
A BGP Route Reflector (RR) is a mechanism in the BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) that simplifies the 
management of BGP in large-scale networks. It allows for reduced configuration complexity and avoids 
the need for a full mesh of BGP connections, which is required in traditional iBGP (Internal BGP) setups.
In traditional iBGP, all routers in an AS (Autonomous System) must form a full mesh of connections with 
one another to exchange routes. This requirement can become impractical as the network grows due to 
high overhead in maintaining a full mesh of connections and configuration complexity as more routers are 
added. BGP Route Reflectors helps in reducing the number of required connections while maintaining 
proper route propagation.
AOS supports BGP Route Reflection for EVPN address families. AOS supports single cluster with 
redundant RRs, and number of leaves on each cluster up to 32.
The connection between RR and the leaves on the overlay is iBGP, and the underlay is IGP (OSPF is 
recommended).
For more information on setting up Route Reflection and Redundant Route Reflectors and its respective 
command parameters and usage guidelines, refer to the “Configuring BGP” and “BGP Commands” 
chapters in the OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide and OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 
CLI Reference Guide.
Below is an example configuration for single cluster with Redundant RR in a BGP EVPN based network.

Route-Reflector and Fabric-VPN (Symmetric IRB) 
Configuration Example
The following is an example of a Symmetric IRB based EVPN network showing route reachability for 
both prefix based and host-based routes.
The example highlights the configuration required to deploy:
• The Route Reflector function
• The Fabric-vpn (symmetric IRB) for host and prefix route reachability.
Figure 18-16 : Route Reflector and Fabric-VPN (Symmetric IRB) Configuration Example
• The two-tier topology depicts an access layer consisting of Leaf/PE nodes (PE-1 to PE4) and a 
distribution layer consisting of Spine nodes (Spine-1 and Spine-2). 
Note: The distribution layer acts as the Route Reflector for BGP EVPN nodes in the access layer.
• A per VRF Fabric-vpn type service is established among the access layer PEs in VRF1 using Fabric-
EVI 50.
• The access layer provides inter-service reachability between multi-homed Host123 attached service 
EVI 123 and single-homed Host-2 attached to service-EVI 40. 
• The access layer switch PE-1 also acts as the border leaf to provide connectivity to the external 
networks. Here, the prefix route 35.35.35.X/24 received on OSPF session on PE-1 VLAN 30 is 
advertised to all the PE nodes of the EVPN network using the BGP EVPN RT-5 route.

remote routes associated with Fabric-EVI 50.

Route-Redistribution for Fabric-EVI Services
Configuration Example
The following is an example of a for Source VRF(s) route redistribution to Fabric EVI along with support 
for route maps.
The configuration example illustrates route redistribution configured for two fabric-EVI (EVI 50 and EVI 
51) services. Here, Fabric EVI 50 is registered to receive routes from its home-VRF ct1. Additionally, it is 
registered to receive routes from VRF ct2 (with route-map filter of ALLROUTES) and from VRF ct3 
(with route-map filter of 132-subnet). Fabric-EVI 51 is registered to receive routes from its home-VRF 
ct2. Additionally, it is registered to receive routes from VRF ct1 (with route-map filter of ALLROUTES).

Underlay Configuration Recommendation for 
BGP EVPN Deployment
For an optimum BGP EVPN session convergence, few underlay configurations are recommended. This 
section highlights those configurations.
A loopback0 address is required, which represents the local PE that will serve as the source IP address of 
the service gateway. PE to PE unicast reachability should be defined through OSPF protocol. BGP should 
be used only as overlay as MP-BGP protocol running EVPN.
The primary role of underlay protocol is to provide fast convergence in event of node failures and network 
link failures. This information should feed into BGP EVPN to trigger path switch for traffic towards MH 
segments in events where one of the PE is not reachable.
Prerequisite 
BFD
While OSPF helps in fast convergence, it alone cannot deliver good convergence numbers. One of the 
important steps towards convergence is to detect failures as soon as possible. 
BFD can help in detecting interface down events in two adjacent OSPF neighbors. BFD can detect failures 
in milliseconds without having to fine tune routing protocol timers. Hence, it is recommended to enable 
BFD on the interfaces where OSPF is enabled.
OSPF
As we recommend using router VLAN based IP interfaces, which minimizes STP in the core, the OSPF 
sessions could be set as point-to-point instead of default multi-point. This eliminates the Default Router 
(DR) election wait times, and sessions are established faster.
After the BFD sessions are established on the interface, configure BFD interoperability with OSPF. This 
means BFD feeds its events into OSPF so that OSPF can trigger the SPF run upon interface down events. 
Even though BFD informs about the events, OSPF acts on those events based on its internal SPF timers. 
For OSPF to act on them immediately, "bfd subsecond" option should be enabled in OSPF context. This 
allows OSPF to act on interface down events from BFD immediately. This option triggers immediate SPF 
run, though only on the area where the interface went down. Its also recommended to run OSPF in only 
one area for EVPN topology.
Apart from the local interface down events when OSPF receives LSA from network, SPF should be 
triggered immediately. This can be achieved by setting SPF timers to zero.
BGP
BGP is enabled only for overlay. MP-BGP for EVPN family is enabled locally and for all BGP peers. 
Only iBGP sessions are supported currently. There should not be any BFD configuration on BGP. When a 
peer is enabled for EVPN, BGP internally registers the peer with IPRM. OSPF informs IPRM about 
reachability for each peer. Once the peer reachability goes down, BGP in the context of EVPN triggers 
peer down event. This event triggers path switch for all the MH segments reachable through backup node.

Configuration Recommendation for Two-Tier 
Topology with RR Redundant Route Reflector (RR)
In a scenario of Leaf and Spine topology with RR enabled, when the direct connection is down, the BGP 
neighbor takes the alternate path, which is not the direct connection. The requirement is to bring the BGP 
neighbor down when the direct connection goes down.
This can be achieved by enabling the TTL-security with maxhops as 0. The switch will send the BGP 
packets with TTL as 255 to that peer. As the maxhops is configured to 0, the BGP packets with a TTL of 
>=255 (255-maxhops) will be accepted. With our recommended configuration, BGP packets received 
from the directly connected peers will be accepted. Any packet that comes through other path will have 
TTL of less than 255, which will not be accepted.
To make the peer react immediately on the interface down event, BFD must be enabled on the BGP peers. 
Subsecond configuration must be avoided on the spine to bring down the BGP peer immediately for the 
interface toggle.
The following diagram and configuration example shows the recommended configuration for two-tier 
topology with RR Redundant Route Reflector (RR).
Consider the direct and indirect paths as given in the topolgy. 
• Direct path: The connection between Leaf1 and Spine1 is through port1 and port7. 
• Indirect Path: The indirect connection between Leaf1 and Spine1 is through port2, port10, port11, 
port4, port3 and port8.

<<<PAGE 638>>>

Route Reflector (RR)

page 18-60
With the below given configuration, when the port1 is disabled, then the BGP peer between Leaf1 and 
Spine1 will go immediately even though there is a above mentioned indirect path. For indirect path, the 
TTL value on the BGP packet received in Spine1 will be 253, which is less than 255 as per the 
expectation. So, the packet will be dropped, and the BGP peer session will not be established even though 
the route is present (indirect path).

EVPN for VXLAN Overlay Service
The OmniSwitch currently supports VXLAN based EVPN. The EVPN works on the control plane and the 
VXLAN works on the data plane. This enhances the Layer 2 and Layer 3 efficiency and scalability. It 
allows to scale the network by extending the Layer 2 connectivity across different location by a network 
overlay in an existing physical network.
The VXLAN based EVPN network will require a spine and leaf-based topology as shown in the figure. 
This tiered topology provides multi-path redundancy for both the CE multihoming and for inter-leaf 
connectivity.
Figure 18-18 : 2-Tier EVPN-VXLAN Network Based on a Spine and Leaf Deployment
The EVPN network depends on a spine and leaf topology for optimum performance. Each Ethernet 
Segment (ES) is guaranteed to have equal cost paths to the peer leaf nodes of the ES from any other leaf in 
the VXLAN network. Thus, EVPN can advertise the ES from different peer VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel End 
Point, the entity that performs the encapsulation and de-encapsulation) / leaf nodes to other / remote leaf 
nodes in the network without having to account for the path costs from remote nodes to the peer VTEPs.
In the above figure, the dual-homed Ethernet Segment Identifier ESI-1 reachability is advertised by both 
the peer VTEPs (Leaf1 and Leaf2) to the other VTEPs/leaf nodes in the network. The reachability to 
ESI-1 using VXLAN EVPN instance (EVI) tunnels has equal cost from all the nodes in the network due to 
the topology of the network.
Each leaf is identified as a PE (Provider Edge). All the nodes (spine and leaf/PE) are identified by the 
Loopback0 interface to establish peer connectivity between the nodes. A BGP peer connectivity is 
established among the leaf nodes. In certain cases, the leaf to spine peer connection is also required (for 
example, Route Reflector in the spine or for multi-site EVPN). The spine nodes will provide the load 
balancing and connectivity between the leaf node (VTEPs), which hosts the single-homed or multi-homed 
ES.

<<<PAGE 642>>>
Configuring EVPN for Overlay Services
EVPN for VXLAN Overlay Service
OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 Network Configuration Guide
December 2025
page 18-64
A 3-tier spine and leaf topology, as shown in the below figure can be used for requirements with hyper 
scalability for Data Center Interconnectivity (DCI). Here, the topology will consist of a super spine layer 
that provides the inter-site gateway functionality. This is especially beneficial when the core network 
(inter-site) is operating in a different overlay protocol (for example, MPLS) or when it is required to have 
a decoupled intra-site and inter-site operation to sustain the complexity of a multi-site EVPN network.
Another variation of the topology can consist of the 3-tier deployment where the CE nodes can be 
represented as an access layer with the overlay network operations in the spine and leaf topology.
Figure 18-19 : 3-Tier EVPN-VXLAN Network Based on a Spine and Leaf Deployment 
with the Super Spine Node

BGP Neighbor Template
The purpose of the BGP neighbor template is to simplify the BGP peer configuration and reduce the 
configuration snapshot size drastically in a case where higher number of peers use the similar 
configuration. 
The individual BGP peer configuration will take precedence over the BGP neighbor template 
configuration. Once the template is applied on the peer, the template configurations will not override the 
existing BGP peer configuration until the individual BGP peer configuration is present. To apply the BGP 
neighbor template configuration on the peer, first remove the individual peer configuration.
This template can be used especially for the spines to configure the number of peers as Route Reflector 
clients in Route Reflector topology (spine and leaf topology) in the EVPN network.
New CLI commands are provided to create new BGP neighbor template. This can be used to create the 
fields for the template. This template can be modified or deleted. The template can be applied on the BGP 
neighbor. The template configuration can be verified by using "show ip bgp nbr-template" and "show 
configuration snapshot bgp" commands. 
Refer to the “BGP Commands” chapter in the OmniSwitch AOS Release 8 CLI Reference Guide for more 
information on how to configure BGP neighbor template for EVPN, and its parameters and usage 
guidelines.
